Pregnancy Nutrition Basics

Why nutrition matters during pregnancy

Pregnancy nutrition supports the growth and development of the baby. A balanced diet can help provide important nutrients such as folate, iron, calcium, vitamin D, protein, and fiber.

Many pregnant women need to focus on regular meals, hydration, safe food choices, and healthy snacks. These habits can support energy levels and help reduce common discomforts.

Important nutrients

Folate helps support early fetal development. Iron supports healthy blood production. Calcium and vitamin D support bones and teeth. Protein supports tissue growth during pregnancy.

Pregnant women should speak with a qualified healthcare professional about prenatal vitamins, supplements, and any special dietary concerns.

Food safety

Food safety is also important during pregnancy. Some foods may carry a higher risk of contamination, so proper washing, cooking, and storage are important.

This article explains general pregnancy nutrition information for educational purposes.

But did you realize your ovaries also feature follicles — and that the amount you have plays a role in your fertility? These tiny sacs, along with your age, hormone levels, and any health conditions you may have, can help predict how likely you are to conceive. </strong><p>If you're trying to get pregnant — or you're just curious about how fertile you actually are — you may hear about certain tests that suggest how likely you are to conceive. One way to learn a little more about what's going on in there is by taking a look at your ovarian follicles.<div id=WhatToExpect_Slideshow data-primis-ad style=margin-top:20px;margin-bottom:20px><script>(function(){function loadPrimis(){var s=document.createElement("script");s.type="text/javascript";s.src="https://live.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?s=121100&cbuster=1782855605047&playerApiId=WhatToExpect_Slideshow";document.getElementById("WhatToExpect_Slideshow").appendChild(s);}
if(window.WTEAdInfo){loadPrimis();}else{window.addEventListener("WTEAdInfoReady",loadPrimis,{once:true});}})();</script></div><p>While they are by no means a crystal ball, here's how your ovarian follicles fit into the whole process of getting pregnant and what they can tell you about your chances.<p><section class=keytakeaways-c><div class=keytakeaways-c__header><div class=keytakeaways-c__header__summary-icon><img src=https://images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/redesign/key_takeaways.svg alt="summary icon" width=24 height=24></div><div class=keytakeaways-c__header__title>Key Takeaways</div></div><div class=keytakeaways-c__body><ul><li><strong>Ovarian follicles are important. </strong>Immature eggs are located in these fluid-filled sacs, and each month, one follicle lets go of an egg during ovulation.<li><strong>A follicle count is revealing. </strong>By tallying the follicles with the help of ultrasound, your doctor can gauge how many eggs you have and learn more about your fertility.<li><strong>Follicle numbers are just part of the picture. </strong>Fertility is affected by many other things, including age, your health, hormone levels, and certain health conditions.</ul></div></section><h2 id=what>What are ovarian follicles?</h2><p>Ovarian follicles are small, fluid-filled sacs in your ovaries that each contain an unfertilized egg. You're born with a set number of eggs and ovarian follicles — usually anywhere from 1 to 2 million — and the total declines over time.<p>By the time you enter puberty, about 25% of these follicles remain, around 300,000. At menopause, fewer than 1,000 ovarian follicles are typically left.<p>Your follicles themselves go through various stages of development. First, primordial follicles will <a href="/pregnancy/fetal-development/fetal-sex-organs-reproductive-system/">form in a fetus's ovaries</a>. They remain that way until puberty, at which point they begin to develop — just like the rest of you — and become primary follicles.<p>Right around the time of ovulation, some of these follicles begin to swell. One will become dominant, and the others that started growing — called antral follicles — will recede.<p>The dominant follicle then breaks open and releases an egg from your ovary, which travels through your fallopian tube toward the uterus. This egg will hang out for about 24 hours, creating an opportunity for <a href=/getting-pregnant/fertility/how-fertilization-happens.aspx>fertilization to occur</a>. The cycle continues each month until you go through menopause.<p>Got more fertility questions? Go to the <a href=https://wte.onelink.me/85iI/7s0l3a5z target=_blank>What to Expect app</a> for smart guides to all things baby-making, plus expert advice and tips from mamas on your same journey.<h2 id=test>What is the antral follicle count test?</h2><p>The antral follicle test is a transvaginal ultrasound that measures how many antral follicles you have. An ultrasound technician or doctor uses a probe inserted into the vagina to examine and count the number of antral follicles on the ovaries. It only takes a few minutes, similar to a pelvic exam.<p>Antral follicles are very small — between 2 to 9 millimeters in diameter — but you can still see them on an ultrasound. The number of antral follicles visible can give your doctor a ballpark sense of how many total eggs (including the many follicles still too small to see) you have remaining in your ovaries.<p>While it's often done on the third day of your menstrual cycle at the same time as other fertility tests, in reality it can be done at any time.<h2 id=normal>How many antral follicles are normal?</h2><p>It depends on your age. If you're older, you'll have fewer antral follicles as someone who's younger. On average, women in their mid 20s to early 30s have around 12 to 30 antral follicles, while women aged 35 to 40 may have between eight and 15, and women aged 41 to 46 may have somewhere between four and 10.<p>If you have fewer than five antral follicles, your doctor may advise certain fertility treatments, like trying in vitro fertilization (IVF) with <a href="/getting-pregnant/fertility-tests-and-treatments/donor-egg/">donor eggs</a>.<h2 id=one>Can you get pregnant with only one mature follicle?</h2><p>If you're trying to conceive naturally, yes, you can get pregnant as long as the follicle releases an egg down the fallopian tube to meet with sperm. But if you're undergoing fertility treatment, it's a little more complicated. It depends on which therapy you're using and how old you are.<p>If you're using <a href="/getting-pregnant/fertility-tests-and-treatments/artificial-insemination-iui/">intrauterine insemination (IUI)</a> and you're under the age of 40, one or two mature follicles is preferred. Having more may not significantly increase your chances of getting pregnant, but it does raise your risk of having <a href=/pregnancy/chances-of-having-twins>twins or multiples</a> if you do get pregnant, <a href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32282611/" target=_blank>one study</a> found.<p>However, women over 40 using IUI may want to consider using ovulation-stimulating treatments that will create more mature follicles. The same research found that women in this age group who had up to four mature follicles tripled their odds of pregnancy without significantly raising their chances of multiples.<p>If you're <a href="/getting-pregnant/ivf/">undergoing IVF</a>, your doctor will also recommend using fertility medications that produce more mature follicles, regardless of your age. You'll receive hormone injections — usually with follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinizing hormone (LH), or both — a couple weeks beforehand to stimulate your ovaries.<p>During the IVF egg retrieval procedure, your doctor uses an ultrasound-guided needle to reach your ovaries and collect the egg from each follicle. Most doctors aim to retrieve more than 10 eggs per cycle.<h2 id=PCOS>How many immature follicles indicate polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)?</h2><p>Women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) — also called polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) — have more antral follicles than women without the condition. It's not unusual for a woman with PCOS to have more than 30 antral follicles total.<p>Women with PCOS produce above-average levels of the hormone testosterone, which hinders ovulation. The follicles struggle to release eggs, so they hang out instead of going through the ovulation process.<p>You can still get <a href="/getting-pregnant/pcos/">pregnant with PCOS</a>, but it may take you longer and you may need to take certain medications, such as metformin, the <a href=/getting-pregnant/fertility-tests-and-treatments/clomid-infertility-treatment>ovulation-inducing drug Clomid</a>, or letrozole. If these types of treatments don't work, IVF can help make pregnancy a reality. Lifestyle changes like losing weight and boosting your vitamin D levels may also help.<p>Keep in mind that an antral follicle count test is one snapshot of your fertility in a moment in time, not the whole picture. Other factors, such as your age, weight, health history, and even genetics play a role, too. <p>The bottom line: Don't stress too much about how many ovarian follicles you have. While they can serve as an indicator of fertility, the exact number is not the be-all and end-all.</p><br></div><div class="medical-authority py-4"><p>From the What to Expect editorial team and <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/about-heidi-murkoff/">Heidi Murkoff,</a> author of <em>What to Expect When You're Expecting</em>. Baby Sprinkle Ideas: Low-Stress Ways to Celebrate Your Next Addition

by Haley Jena
Fact-Checked by Caroline Picard

If this isn’t your first child but you still want to celebrate your upcoming arrival, a baby sprinkle might be for you.
Back to Top
In This Article
  • What is a baby sprinkle?
  • How should you throw a baby sprinkle shower?
  • What should you put on your baby sprinkle registry?

A baby sprinkle is a relaxed, low-key way to celebrate your family’s upcoming addition without all of the hustle and bustle that comes with a traditional baby shower. These celebrations tend to be more focused on support and connection rather than lots of gifts. Guest lists for baby sprinkles are usually smaller, décor is simple, and registries focus on basic essentials.

When you were pregnant with your first child, a loved one may have thrown you a big baby shower to celebrate your bundle on the way. If you're expecting again, you'll undoubtedly be just as excited for your second (or third, or fourth …) arrival — but you may be looking for a more low-key gathering. A baby sprinkle can be the perfect solution.

Here's everything expectant parents and their hosts need to know about these events.

Key Takeaways
  • A baby sprinkle is a casual, intimate alternative to a traditional baby shower. These celebrations are typically smaller, less formal, and focused on support rather than big gifts, since parents likely already have most essentials.
  • Registry items for a baby sprinkle tend to be smaller necessities like diapers and onesies, though bigger items may be appropriate if there's a large age gap or gear needs refreshing.
  • Baby sprinkle activities can be simple and personal — from advice cards and DIY onesies to games that involve older siblings — making the event feel warm without requiring elaborate planning.

What is a baby sprinkle?

The name says it all: Instead of a bigger party where first-time parents are showered with gifts, a baby sprinkle is a more casual, relaxed gathering where the guests of honor are "sprinkled" with support and potentially smaller gifts.

The concept of baby sprinkles is relatively new, so the host may need to clarify what the event entails on the invitation. Baby sprinkles are quickly growing in popularity, though, with more seasoned parents participating in the fun trend.

Although there are no official rules about what should happen at a baby shower versus a sprinkle, the two events might look something like this:

  • A baby shower is often more formal, features a variety of games and decorations, and has a bigger guest list. Because first-time parents need so much new gear, a traditional shower usually includes a full baby registry. 
  • A baby sprinkle is usually more casual than a traditional shower and focuses on surrounding the seasoned parents with warmth and love. Since the guests of honor likely already own most big-ticket items, the registry might include smaller essentials such as diapers, wipes, and onesies.

"My mom and sister are hosting [a baby sprinkle], but it's just in a park, with like donuts and coffee, super quiet, super chill. We did do a registry but just for the necessities (double stroller, second camera for monitor, diapers)," says What to Expect Community mom cmgskj625.

"This is my second child and we are doing a 'baby and brunch' theme this go around," says Community mom MKCMRJC2124. "This one will be more relaxed with yard games instead of the traditional baby shower games."

How should you throw a baby sprinkle shower?

There's no right or wrong way to have a baby sprinkle, but there are a few things hosts should keep in mind when planning this event: 

Think about the timing

Many expectant parents prefer to have baby showers or sprinkles in the second or early- to mid-third trimester, since that leaves plenty of time to create a baby registry but isn't too close to the due date. Ultimately, though, it's up to the host and expectant parents to decide on timing.

Don't forget to give guests plenty of time to plan for the sprinkle, too. A good rule of thumb is to send invitations at least four weeks in advance.

Plan the guest list

Sprinkle showers are often more about support and advice than big gifts, and these events tend to have a more casual, intimate tone. For that reason, many parents like to keep their sprinkle guest list on the smaller side, inviting close friends and family. If you'd like to make your baby sprinkle a coed event, that's an increasingly popular (and fun!) choice too. 

Send the invitations

When it comes to baby sprinkle invites, don't worry too much about formality. If the host wants to mail traditional invitations, that’s totally fine, but know that a email invite works well, too. Baby sprinkle etiquette usually recommends that you not include registry information on the invite, but have it handy for those who ask (no doubt a few will!).

Choose a theme

Since baby sprinkles are usually informal, the host doesn't need to go all-out with elaborate decorations, fancy invites, and gift bags. While it's not necessary to choose a specific theme, many parents and hosts find that it does help make decorating easy.

A popular idea is to capitalize on "sprinkles" and have a sundae or cupcake bar with all different colors and types of — you guessed it! — sprinkles. You can print "Sprinkle a lot of love!" on colorful invitations.

Select decorations

Because a baby sprinkle shower is usually more casual, you don't need lots of elaborate decorations (unless you want them!). Many hosts opt for simple decor, such as a few flowers, balloons, and sweet photos.

And if the baby sprinkle is a virtual event, consider sending guests a fun Zoom background to make it feel extra-special.

Plan the baby sprinkle menu

For this simpler party, you might keep the menu light, with bite-size hors d'oeuvres, snacks, sweets, and punch. Think: pregnancy-safe cheese with crackers, a yogurt bar with fruit and candies, veggies and dips, nuts and olives, or brownies and cake.

Not only will this make party prep relatively effortless, it will give guests an opportunity to mix and mingle while they load their plates.

Consider activities and games

While traditional baby shower games still work at a sprinkle, you can plan on simpler activities, too, like making a DIY shower gift as a group. Put the emphasis on those nearest and dearest to the parent-to-be. A few ideas to add a personal touch to the party:

  • Ask guests to write their best advice for the sibling on slips of paper, which can be turned into a keepsake book. This is also a great way to make the big brother or sister feel included.
  • Make a no-sew quilt with outgrown clothing or blankets belonging to the older siblings or cousins.
  • Decorate a plain baby book, and ask guests to write a note to the baby inside.
  • Use fabric markers, stamp pads, and stencils to create personalized onesies.
  • Make adorable homemade headbands for your little one using lace and ribbons.
  • Distribute printable games listing celebrity parents and the names of their babies for guests to match up.
  • Print letters of the alphabet on sheets of paper and have guests decorate them for your little one (for example, "K is for Kitty"; "C is for Caterpillar"). Be sure to remind them to sign their names on the back so it doubles as a guest book!
  • Ask guests to write a funny saying or message on the front waistband of a diaper. Then, stash the diapers away in a cute bin to be reserved only for middle-of-the-night changes. That way, you'll have a little comic relief and positivity during those wee-hour-changes.

Involve older siblings

A new baby is exciting, but it can also be anxiety-provoking for older kids. You can help ease the transition by involving them in this event, such as by assigning them a special job during the planning process or giving them a small gift "from" their new sibling.

And if you’re planning a sip-and-see party after baby is born, invite the older sibling to help introduce the new baby to everyone.

What should you put on your baby sprinkle registry?

Although you may not think a baby registry is necessary this time around, it can still be helpful for guests, since a registry takes the guesswork out of buying gifts. Unlike a traditional baby shower, seasoned parents likely have most baby essentials, and many second- or third-time parents opt to add smaller gifts to their baby sprinkle registries.

However, other families may need to register for bigger items (for example, if there's a big age gap between siblings and the parents need to stock up on newborn gear all over again).

A few ideas to consider adding to your baby sprinkle registry, depending on your situation:

  • Diapering products: Request basics that you'll need right away and will go through quickly, such as diapers, diaper cream, and wipes. Making a diaper cake or hosting a diaper raffle can make this gifting staple seem more fun.
  • Baby clothes: They might be especially useful if the new baby is a different sex than the older child or due at a different time of year. Even if you have plenty of hand-me-downs, consider registering for clothes in sizes 12 months and larger: While they may not be in use for a while, that's the age when clothes start to get more wear and tear, and previously worn styles may be less useful.
  • Products for multiple children: For example, if the older child still likes riding in her stroller, you may need to upgrade to a double or convertible stroller, or invest in accessories like a second seat or toddler stroller board to extend the life of your current model.
  • Refreshed gear: This might include car seats (they expire, and you shouldn't reuse even a relatively new one if it has been in a crash, is missing parts or has been recalled), cribs (especially if the older sibling is still using the one you have), or small breast pump and bottle parts that might no longer be in the best condition.
  • Support for parents: Think food delivery gift cards for those nights when cooking feels impossible.

or in-person, a hospital tour is one of the simplest ways to calm any pre-birth jitters and feel prepared. Usually scheduled around the start of the third trimester, these free visits take expectant parents through the registration process and key areas of the maternity ward, while giving you a chance to ask questions.</strong><p dir=ltr>After all, no matter how long you've got until your due date, it's normal to be excited — and a bit nervous — about what goes down once labor starts. What’s more, if you’re not used to hospitals, staying in one might feel a little intimidating.<div id=WhatToExpect_Slideshow data-primis-ad style=margin-top:20px;margin-bottom:20px><script>(function(){function loadPrimis(){var s=document.createElement("script");s.type="text/javascript";s.src="https://live.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?s=121100&cbuster=1782858556603&playerApiId=WhatToExpect_Slideshow";document.getElementById("WhatToExpect_Slideshow").appendChild(s);}
if(window.WTEAdInfo){loadPrimis();}else{window.addEventListener("WTEAdInfoReady",loadPrimis,{once:true});}})();</script></div><p dir=ltr><span id=docs-internal-guid-6651dbfb-7fff-3b37-d1d1-328d053473fe>Here’s more about what you’ll learn during a hospital tour when you're pregnant, plus some key questions you can ask.</span><p dir=ltr><section class=keytakeaways-c><div class=keytakeaways-c__header><div class=keytakeaways-c__header__summary-icon><img src=https://images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/redesign/key_takeaways.svg alt="summary icon" width=24 height=24></div><div class=keytakeaways-c__header__title>Key Takeaways</div></div><div class=keytakeaways-c__body><ul><li>Taking a hospital tour in the third trimester can help you familiarize yourself with logistics like parking, entrance points, and registration before you arrive to give birth.<li>Both in-person and virtual tours can cover essential ground — from triage and labor suites to postpartum rooms and the newborn nursery — providing a realistic preview of the delivery experience.<li>Hospital tours are also an opportunity to ask any questions you have about pain management options, visitor policies, birthing amenities, and support services like breastfeeding assistance.</ul></div></section><h2 id=necessary>Is a hospital tour necessary?</h2><p><span id=docs-internal-guid-3a623616-7fff-7795-6484-19b1d34d6238>A hospital or <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/birth-center/">birthing center</a> tour can pay off in a number of ways. If it’s in person, it can be a great practice run for getting to the hospital when you’re actually in labor. You can figure out the best route to take — which means you can (mostly) be on auto-pilot when it’s go time (no worries about a GPS failure).</span><p dir=ltr>You can also iron out other details during an in-person or virtual hospital tour — like where to park and what entrance to go to, whether you get there at lunchtime, during rush hour, or in the middle of the night. During an in-person visit, you may even get to meet some of the staff who will be helping you during your hospital stay, which can be comforting.<span id=1-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#1 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#1>KidsHealth From Nemours</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>Where Should I Have My Baby?</span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=1-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[1]</a></sup><p dir=ltr>But perhaps the biggest benefit of a pre-delivery maternity tour, either virtually or in person, is that it gives you a sneak peek of where you’ll be and what will happen on the big day.<p dir=ltr>"We did a tour a few weeks ago," says <a href="https://community.whattoexpect.com/forums/" rel="">What to Expect Community</a> mom emmlou29. "The nurse who showed us around was super nice and explained everything. Gave me a lot of peace about going to give birth."<p dir=ltr>"I did a virtual tour with my daughter, [I] mainly just wanted to see where to go so there was no confusion day of," says mom AL2019.<h2 id=when>When should you take a hospital tour? </h2><p dir=ltr>A good time to take a hospital tour is at the beginning of the <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/third-trimester-of-pregnancy.aspx rel="">third trimester</a> of pregnancy, in <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/week-by-week/week-28.aspx rel="">month 7</a>. More specifically, you could take the tour between <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/week-by-week/week-30.aspx rel="">week 30</a> and <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/week-by-week/week-34.aspx rel="">week 34</a> of pregnancy.<p dir=ltr>Hospital tours are free, and setting one up is easy: Call the hospital or birthing center (or check the website to find dates and times of upcoming tours) and reserve your spot.<span id=2-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#2 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#2>UCLA Health</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>BirthPlace Tours </span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=2-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[2]</a></sup><p dir=ltr>Ever since the COVID-19 pandemic, virtual hospital tours have also become more common. Both in-person and virtual tours offer a lot of good information. <p>To take a virtual hospital tour, which is typically self-paced with 360-degree views, visit the facility’s website. A virtual tour typically includes the lobby, admissions, most of the floor plans, operating rooms and various departments. <p>Most virtual hospital tours also feature detailed captions with every picture, plus an FAQ section.<h2 id=learn>What can you learn during a hospital tour?</h2><p dir=ltr>Wondering what happens during an in-person hospital tour? You’ll want to set aside about an hour for the tour, which usually involves a labor and delivery nurse or hospital educator who’s tasked with walking you through the whole delivery process, from admission to discharge. Here's what you'll likely see during this tour:<ul><li dir=ltr><strong>The registration desk:</strong> The first stop will probably be the registration office. If you haven’t pre-registered already, circle back and do so after the tour — getting all the paperwork out of the way will make your admission process faster.<li dir=ltr><strong>The triage area: </strong>Though you may not get to enter, you’ll likely get a look at the triage area. That’s the pre-delivery part of the maternity ward, where a nurse will monitor your vitals and assess whether delivery is imminent.<li dir=ltr><strong>Other essential rooms:</strong> You'll also get a sneak peek of the family waiting rooms, a labor and delivery suite, and a postpartum room. If the center has private and semi-private rooms, ask to see both. The best part is usually last when you’ll get to see the newborn nursery, so get ready to ooh and ahh over the little cuties.</ul><p dir=ltr>Keep in mind that delivery wards can be intense places: There are tears, nervous spouses, well-meaning grandparents, and actual screams sometimes. It can be a lot to take in — but remember, it's all in the excitement of bringing a new life into the world, so don’t be scared!<h2 id=questions>What questions should you ask during a hospital or birthing center tour?</h2><p>The nurse or hospital educator will provide lots of valuable information, but don’t be afraid to speak up about something that’s on your mind. Here are some questions to ask on a hospital or birth center tour:<ul><li>Insurance plans vary, of course, but what are the fees for private rooms and special birthing facilities?<li>What should I <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/checklist/hospital-packing.aspx>pack in my hospital bag</a>?<li>What <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/labor-pain/">pain management options</a> are available?<li>Are you equipped to care for preterm infants, multiples, and high-risk pregnancies?<li>What birthing amenities does the hospital offer (such as a <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/labor-and-delivery/delivery-options/labor-positions.aspx>birth ball, birthing tub, or squat bar</a>)?<li>Who can be in the room during the delivery? Is there a limit on the number of people?<li>Are recording devices (like a video camera and tripod or cellphone) allowed in the delivery room?<li>Can I play music, light a scented candle, or have other mood-enhancing items in my room?<li>Do you work with a cord blood bank (if you’re considering <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/cord-blood/what-is-cord-blood-banking/">banking your baby’s cord blood</a>)? If not, how can I arrange to transfer my baby’s cord blood?<span id=3-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#3 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#3>American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>Cord Blood Banking</span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=3-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[3]</a></sup><li>When are the visiting hours? Can children visit?<li>Is my partner allowed to stay with me overnight?<li>Can my baby stay in the room with me during our stay instead of in the nursery?<li>What other security policies are in place?<li>Do you offer breastfeeding support services?<li>What kind of information will I go home with?</ul><p dir=ltr>If you have other questions or concerns, your doctor or the hospital staff will be more than glad to address them. And don’t worry about sounding silly — the physicians and nurses have heard them all before and are happy to help. <p dir=ltr>Enjoy your hospital tour, whether it’s virtual or in-person, and remember, everyone has the same goal: to make sure your baby has a healthy entrance into the world!<p><div class=jw-video-player-wrapper data-video-id=YqjITDUn data-placement=Inline><div id=jw-video-player-YqjITDUn class=jw-player></div></div><div class="wbw-video__info d-flex justify-content-center mb-3"><span class="wbw-video__info__title text-center"></span></div></p><br></div><div class="medical-authority py-4"><p>From the What to Expect editorial team and <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/about-heidi-murkoff/">Heidi Murkoff,</a> author of <em>What to Expect When You're Expecting</em>. Whether you're after a quick one-liner or sentimental story, pregnancy announcement captions can come in every style — funny, sweet, or deeply personal. Below are options for every situation, from first pregnancies and multiples to rainbow babies and IVF journeys, plus seasonal ideas and quotes for extra inspiration.

After weeks and weeks of waiting to publicly share your adorable not-so-little secret, announcing your pregnancy can feel exhilarating. While some parents have been leaning into the trend of not sharing the news on social media and hard launching their baby after they're born, others (myself included!) may be eager to post about their exciting news. 

And if you’re still riding the emotional high (or nerves!) of seeing those two pink lines, download the What to Expect app to track early symptoms and connect with other expectant parents going through the same first-flutter feelings.

But what do you actually say when you post about your soon-to-be bundle of joy? Is your caption simple, sappy, sentimental, or sweet? "My timeline and newsfeed is FULL of pregnancy announcements," says What to Expect Community mom Milz5421. "I haven’t posted mine because I have no idea how I want to announce!"

Pregnancy announcement captions can be as simple as “We’re expecting!” or a more detailed explanation of the journey that led to those two little lines on the pregnancy test. Here's some caption inspiration to spark your creativity. 

Key Takeaways
  • Pregnancy announcement captions may be short and punny or long and heartfelt — the tone is entirely up to you, whether you're going funny, sentimental, or detailed about your journey.
  • You might consider captions tailored to specific circumstances, such as rainbow babies, fertility treatment journeys, multiples, and seasonal or holiday announcements.
  • While some parents these days opt to skip social media announcements altogether and "hard launch" after birth, plenty of caption inspiration exists for those who do want to share the news with friends and family online.

What is a pregnancy announcement caption? 

A pregnancy announcement caption is the text attached to a photo or video you share on social media. It could also be a one-liner shown on a letterboard or other sign featured in a social media post. Depending on the theme and your own personality, the caption can be short and snappy, long and detailed, or loaded up with silly pregnancy puns… you name it, the options are endless.

What are some short and sweet pregnancy announcement captions?

jolieeeb via Instagram

  1. “in our mom and dad era” —@jolieeeb

  2. “I’m in love with a human I haven’t met yet”

  3. “And then there were three…”

  4. “Baby loading…”

  5. “Oh BABY”

  6. “Oh BOY”

  7. “Half of you and half of me”

  8. “Our greatest adventure is about to begin”

What are some more detailed pregnancy announcement caption ideas?

sadekelly_ via Instagram

  1. “I'm pleased to announce that my incredible wife Helen is pregnant with our second child, a baby boy, due July 2024. This pregnancy hasn’t been an easy one. Two failed embryo transfers with this transfer being our second to last one. Even then we were told this baby was unlikely to survive. At the two week scan (viability scan) the baby was too small to measure. But here we are 20 weeks later, and it’s finally starting to feel. This year has taught us both a lot when it comes to the emotional pain that surrounds trying to conceive and our hearts go out to all those who have or are currently experiencing similar struggles.” — insideoursuitcase

  2. “I’m pregnant! again! 2 under 2, here we go! Send prayers but really though, but we couldn’t be more excited — this is a dream come true for us. any mamas, papas or caregivers who’ve gone from 1 to 2 kids, please share your wisdom. also, so open to your your wisdom around kids that are ~22 months apart. even though I’ve never been drawn to kids, becoming a mama has felt like the most natural, fulfilling thing I’ve ever done. our 16-month-old is a firecracker and the most hilarious, magnetic, and attuned little human I’ve ever met. just witnessing her become more of herself each day is the biggest gift. we’re so excited to begin this journey again and I simply can’t wait to meet the next one. who will she be?! this second pregnancy has already been SO different than the first. I’m so much more tired, more anxious, more nauseous, and I keep forgetting I’m pregnant because I’m so consumed with my toddler. although second trimester vibes just hit and I couldn’t be happier to be here” — erinclairejones     

  3. “Every kick, every flutter, and every tiny heartbeat reminds us that our lives are about to change in the most incredible way. We’re so excited to share that we’re expecting! #Summer2024” — @sadekelly_

  2. “There’s a little bun in the oven!” — @sprinkledsugarcookies 

  3. “Here we GROW again!” — @_sierraroth_ 

  4. “Alexa, play ‘Baby’ by Justin Bieber”

  5. “Oops…we did it again”

  6. “We’ve been cooking something up”

  7. “A little cutie is on the way”

What are some rainbow baby announcement captions?

_allisontravis via Instagram

  1. “After every storm there is a rainbow”

  2. “My rainbow, my everything”

  3. “Oh hello, little rainbow”

  4. “Although these pictures show the hands down happiest moment in my life, I know how incredibly hard announcements like these are for those struggling with loss and pregnancy troubles. After multiple back-to-back losses, lots of testing and multiple surgeries, l feel you and understand the sadness & disappointment you are feeling. Absolutely no one deserves to endure that pain. Please stay positive and know I am praying for you. I am always a shoulder you can lean on.” — @_allisontravis

What are some baby announcement ideas following fertility treatments?

lauracbelike via Instagram

  1. “Worth every shot”

  2. “Made with lots of love and a little science”

  3. “The little embryo that could”

  4. “You were worth the wait little one” — @lauracbeilke

  5. “After over 3 years of trials, we are so excited to announce BABY GIRL ERHARD will be joining us January 2024" — @oakgrovefarmstn

  6. “The most joyful personal news I’ve ever had the privilege to share. We’re finally going to be parents. The journey to get to this day has been silent yet incredibly long and arduous after first being told we would never have children. It evolved into recurrent miscarriages, multiple IVF egg retrievals, an endometriosis diagnosis and hours long surgery and finally the discovery of reproductive immunology and alloimmunity and the importance of personal advocacy. We are forever grateful to the 5 incredible doctors and multiple nurses for giving us a chance. We knew there always was one.” — melorlinstv

What are some twin or multiples pregnancy announcement captions?

insideno.48 via Instagram

  2. “The best things in life are THREE”

  3. “Two more peas are joining our pod”

  4. “A year ago we said I do, now we’re expecting two” - amyshomelife

What are some quotes to include in a pregnancy announcement caption?

  1. “If I’m thinking correctly,” said Pooh “a new baby is probably, undoubtedly, the grandest gift that could ever be.” — A.A. Milne 

  2. “You know what the great thing about babies is? They are like little bundles of hope. Like the future in a basket.” — Lish McBride

  3. “Words can not express the joy of new life.” — Hermann Hesse

  4. “A new baby is like the beginning of all things wonder, hope, a dream of possibilities.” — Eda J. LeShan

How To Turn Your Ultrasound Into a Forever Keepsake

by Blake Bakkila
Fact-Checked by Melissa Bykofsky

Courtney Grayden
Creative ideas for those precious photos.
Back to Top
In This Article
  • Laminate them
  • Hand-stitch your little love
  • Compile them in a framed collage
  • Use them in your baby book
  • Make a holiday memento

During a recent post-move cleanout, I came upon my collection of sonograms from my pregnancy. I used one of the photo strips for my maternity shoot, but three years later, they are just collecting dust in my son’s keepsake box. 

I wasn’t ready to throw these away, so I began to research what other moms do with these prints, and it turns out there are many creative ways to preserve your ultrasound photos. Some of these ideas are for seasoned crafters, while others take just five minutes to recreate with items you might already have at home. It’s easy to make something you and your family will cherish for years.

Laminate them

Courtney Grayden

If you plan to keep these photos out on display, laminating them will help prevent the ink from fading. 

“We used cold lamination to protect the pictures from fading and we keep them in an album,” says WTE Community member daniiiiela. “Make sure you keep them away from sunlight and heat. I never thought someone might wanna throw them away. I want my grandkids to see them too.”

Once carefully laminated, moms are also turning them into giftable keepsakes. 

After placing her sonogram for her first child into a laminating pouch, Courtney Grayden punched a hole at the top and tied an “It’s a boy!” ribbon onto it. “I wanted to give our close family members a simple yet special little keepsake,” she says. “Even though they didn’t attend my ultrasound appointments, the sonograms made those miraculous moments tangible for them.” It also took her less than five minutes — win-win!

Hand-stitch your little love

Allison Furlong

Calling all embroidery gurus! Allison Furlong, the creative behind @thenavystudio, wanted a keepsake that would never fade. The talented embroiderer who sells her work on The Navy Studio website decided to make her very first ultrasound embroidery using her own baby’s sonogram. 

She says hand embroidery is a slow craft if you're interested in giving it a try. “Every tiny stitch — the repetitive motion of pushing the needle through the fabric — forces your breathing to slow down and for your brain to quiet down as you concentrate,” she explains.

Fortunately, she adds that it’s an affordable craft, too. “Any fabric will do (I use thrifted cotton shirts, pillow cases, etc.),” she says. “All supplies can be purchased at a local craft store for less than $10.” 

She suggests sketching out the ultrasound on the fabric in pencil or chalk as your guide for the stitches. “If you make a mistake, just cut out the stitches and try again,” she adds. “Practice makes perfect, and going slow is key!”

Compile them in a framed collage

Natalie MacRitchie

Natalie MacRitchie (@natalie_macritchie), a mom of two, took nine of her sonograms and put them into one large frame. “So much of pregnancy goes by in a blur, and these little snapshots are the moments that made everything feel real — the first tiny heartbeat, the first little profile, the milestones that we didn’t want tucked away in a drawer,” she says. “Having them displayed like this is a reminder of how far we’ve come as a family, and it’s something my kids can look at one day and know how loved they were from the very beginning.”

To replicate this keepsake, MacRitchie recommends purchasing a frame with individual slots or pin-boardsthat will keep your sonograms flat and protected. And if you’re concerned about them fading, especially if your frame will get a lot of direct sunlight, make copies of them to place in the frame. Bonus tip: MacRitchie wrote down the date on the back of each to remember the exact appointment each sonogram was from.

Use them in your baby book

Jennise Valerio

Jennise Valerio, a WTE community parent, is carrying on a meaningful tradition started by her parents: scrapbooks for each child. “Feeling the pages between my fingers, the scent of the paper, seeing my mom’s handwriting, seeing original copies of my awards and achievements…nothing compares,” she says. “I wanted to make sure my son has something physical he can look back on whenever he wants to, regardless of how technology evolves.”

Valerio visits Walgreens for affordable photo prints, and of course, she features her sonogram in the scrapbook, too. Her number one piece of advice: Don’t stress. “There’s no rush,” she says. “Work on them in your spare time. Have your projects stored together for easy retrieval, and work on your albums during the baby’s naptime or after bedtime.” 

Make a holiday memento

Kirsten Robinson

Kirsten Robinson, a mom of two from Bozeman, Montana, purchased a hollow glass ball ornament that was designed to be decorated and filled with ribbon or sequins, and then hung on the tree. She says she used it to “bottle up her baby’s little firsts.” Among the baby items Robinson placed inside was a sonogram from her now 4-year-old's 30 week appointment. 

“This craft was extra special this year because I made it with my 4-year-old and added her ultrasound photos and hospital bracelets and one of her pacifiers,” she says. “She asked so many questions about pregnancy and her arrival!”

class=article-body><p><strong>Obstructive sleep apnea is a breathing-related disorder that can occur during pregnancy as a result of hormonal shifts, weight gain, and reduced lung capacity. This condition causes your breathing to start and stop repeatedly during sleep and deprives your body of oxygen, which can be serious for both you and your baby on board. Symptoms are manageable with lifestyle changes, breathing aids, or a CPAP machine, and often improve after giving birth.</strong><p>If you’re like most expectant women, you’re probably already finding it harder and harder to sleep now that you’re growing a baby. More than three-quarters of all pregnant women say they experience more sleep disturbances than usual — and while it may make for one tired mom-to-be, it’s still considered very normal. But obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) can be more serious than typical sleep disruptions.<span id=1-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#1 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#1>Sleep Foundation</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>Sleep Apnea</span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=1-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[1]</a></sup><div id=WhatToExpect_Slideshow data-primis-ad style=margin-top:20px;margin-bottom:20px><script>(function(){function loadPrimis(){var s=document.createElement("script");s.type="text/javascript";s.src="https://live.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?s=121100&cbuster=1782858567204&playerApiId=WhatToExpect_Slideshow";document.getElementById("WhatToExpect_Slideshow").appendChild(s);}

And if you’ve already been diagnosed with OSA, treatment can help you get more of the sleep both you and your developing baby need.</span><p dir=ltr><section class=keytakeaways-c><div class=keytakeaways-c__header><div class=keytakeaways-c__header__summary-icon><img src=https://images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/redesign/key_takeaways.svg alt="summary icon" width=24 height=24></div><div class=keytakeaways-c__header__title>Key Takeaways</div></div><div class=keytakeaways-c__body><ul><li><strong>Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is more common during pregnancy</strong> due to hormonal changes, weight gain, and increased pressure on the diaphragm. Having OSA can raise a mom-to-be's risk of gestational diabetes and preeclampsia.<li><strong>Warning signs for OSA</strong> can include loud snoring, gasping during sleep, daytime fatigue, morning headaches, and mood changes.<li><strong>Obstructive sleep apnea treatments</strong> range from lifestyle adjustments (such as sleeping on your side or using saline sprays) to CPAP machines, and symptoms often improve after delivery.</ul></div></section><h2 id=causes>What causes obstructive sleep apnea?</h2><p><a target=_blank rel="nofollow noopener"><div class=media-c><img data-src='//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/Obstructive-sleep-apnea-2020.gif?width=596' alt='obstructive sleep apnea medical illustration' width=596 height=335 class='__lazy-load hero-img embed-image'></div></a><p dir=ltr>Sleep apnea is the most severe form of sleep-disordered breathing conditions.<span id=2-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#2 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#2>Obstetrics and Gynecology Clinics of North America</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>Management of Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Pregnancy</span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=2-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[2]</a></sup> This is a chronic condition that occurs when the upper airways collapse during sleep, temporarily blocking airflow and causing interruptions in ventilation, or the movement and exchange of deoxygenated for oxygenated air. Temporary pauses in breathing, called apneas, can last anywhere from 10 seconds to a minute or more. <p dir=ltr>The level of sleep apnea you have is based on the number of times you stop breathing in your sleep. Here's how it's classified:<ul><li dir=ltr><strong>Mild sleep apnea:</strong> five to 14 pauses in breathing an hour<li dir=ltr><strong>Moderate sleep apnea:</strong> 15 to 29 pauses in an hour<li dir=ltr><strong>Severe sleep apnea:</strong> More than 30 episodes an hour</ul><p dir=ltr>Obstructive sleep apnea is actually one of three types of apnea. The others are <strong>central sleep apnea (CSA)</strong>, which occurs when the brain has trouble controlling the muscles necessary for taking in air, leading to slower and more shallow breathing; and <strong>mixed or complex sleep apnea</strong>, which<strong> </strong>is a combination of both OSA and CSA at the same time. This type of sleep apnea is usually diagnosed overnight when events can be recorded.<p dir=ltr>Apnea is often accompanied by a pattern of heavy <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/symptoms-and-solutions/snoring.aspx rel="">snoring</a>, which gets louder just before it quiets completely while the airflow stops. After a few seconds, the body reacts to the temporary lack of air with a loud snort or gasp, and then the snoring resumes.<p dir=ltr>"The further along [in pregnancy] I get, my hubby tells me I snore loud and there’s pauses at times in my breathing," says <a href="https://community.whattoexpect.com/forums/" rel="">What to Expect Community</a> mom Ricanprincess99.<p dir=ltr>Typically, people with apnea don’t wake up fully and don’t remember these episodes, though their quality of sleep is greatly affected.<h2 id=who>Who is at risk of obstructive sleep apnea?</h2><p><span id=docs-internal-guid-e44f097e-7fff-2efe-d6dc-297708339cb0>All pregnant women have an increased risk of obstructive sleep apnea due to normal physiologic changes, including hormonal changes. For example, higher levels of estrogen during pregnancy can cause the mucus membranes in your nose to swell, <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/symptoms-and-solutions/nasal-congestion.aspx>leading to nasal congestion</a>, which effectively narrows your breathing airway. </span><p><span id=docs-internal-guid-e44f097e-7fff-2efe-d6dc-297708339cb0>Also, as pregnancy progresses, the pressure of the uterus on your diaphragm leads to a decrease in lung function residual capacity (the volume of air you have left in your lungs after you breathe out). This reduced capacity contributes to an increased collapsibility of your airways.</span><p dir=ltr>If you’re overweight, obese, or gained more than the <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/gaining-too-much-weight/">recommended amount of weight during pregnancy</a>, you’re particularly at risk of obstructive sleep apnea. Extra tissue in your neck can block your airway and make it harder to breathe at night. Moms-to-be with <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/pregnancy-health/gestational-diabetes/" rel="">gestational diabetes</a> are also at higher risk.<p dir=ltr><span id=docs-internal-guid-e68d6231-7fff-eff7-7ec1-845190bfb27f>Other reasons your airway may collapse or become blocked during sleep include <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/pregnancy-health/allergies-during-pregnancy/">congestion caused by allergies</a> or illness, along with certain physical attributes, like a receding chin, enlarged adenoids, a large tongue, a deviated septum, or an above-average neck circumference.</span><h2 id=risks>What are the risks of obstructive sleep apnea during pregnancy?</h2><p dir=ltr>Over time, sleep apnea lowers your blood oxygen levels. The less air you breathe in each night, the less oxygen your body gets. This condition not only causes fatigue but can also increase your risk of high blood pressure, cardiovascular problems, and other serious health conditions. <p dir=ltr><span id=docs-internal-guid-328a7a9d-7fff-8191-8216-e60eff5b96fa>Pregnant women with sleep apnea may also be more likely to develop conditions that affect their babies’ health, like gestational diabetes and <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/preeclampsia/" rel="">preeclampsia</a>, another reason it’s so vital to be diagnosed and treated as soon as possible by your doctor.</span><h2 id=signs>What are the warning signs of sleep apnea?</h2><p dir=ltr><span id=docs-internal-guid-166d0607-7fff-81d4-11b6-2c8b8e23f646>While only your partner may hear <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/symptoms-and-solutions/snoring.aspx>your loud snoring</a> and sudden gasps for air at night, you should clock how fatigued you feel during the day. Also, make sure to note whether you often fall asleep while reading, watching TV, or working at the computer, or if you’re feeling especially irritable, impatient, and forgetful. Sleepiness and moodiness during the day are signs of sleep apnea.</span><p>Other signs of OSA include waking up with a headache, sore throat, or dry mouth; nighttime sweating; and a decreased libido. So if you find yourself popping a Tylenol as soon as you get out of bed, sleep apnea may be the culprit.<span id=3-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#3 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#3>Mayo Clinic</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>Obstructive Sleep Apnea</span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=3-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[3]</a></sup><p dir=ltr>To diagnose sleep apnea, your doctor will evaluate your signs and symptoms and examine your mouth, nose, and throat.<span id=4-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#4 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#4>The Texas Heart Institute</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>Obstructive Sleep Apnea</span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=4-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[4]</a></sup><p dir=ltr><span id=docs-internal-guid-e430a511-7fff-14d3-7b95-fce42d7cf262>Your practitioner may then refer you to a sleep specialist for another test called a polysomnography. This study — done at home or in a lab — measures your airflow, breathing patterns, blood oxygen levels, and other factors while you’re asleep to confirm if what you have is in fact sleep apnea.  </span><h2 id=treatment>How is obstructive sleep apnea treated?</h2><p dir=ltr>Treatment for sleep apnea usually starts with lifestyle changes. Your doctor may advise you not to sleep on your back. You may be able to arrange pillows or a <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/baby-products/pregnancy/best-body-pillows-pregnancy/" rel="">pregnancy pillow</a> to support your back. If you just can’t seem to stay off it, though, try taping a tennis ball to the back of your pajama top so that when you roll over, the ball reminds you to stay on your side.<p dir=ltr>Other solutions your practitioner may recommend for obstructive sleep apnea include:<ul><li dir=ltr><span id=docs-internal-guid-51821191-7fff-03a0-d6a6-0ab01d757f4f><strong>Over-the-counter products: </strong>Adhesive breathing strips can open up the nostrils for easier breathing. </span><span id=docs-internal-guid-51821191-7fff-03a0-d6a6-0ab01d757f4f>For apnea caused by congestion, try a saline spray or rinse, a humidifier, or an OTC decongestant (but talk to your doctor first about all these to ensure they’re safe).</span><li dir=ltr><strong>Maintaining a healthy pregnancy weight: </strong>If you’re overweight or obese, work with your health care provider on a weight management plan. Being at a healthy weight can really help with sleep apnea.<span id=5-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#5 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#5>American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>Obesity and Pregnancy</span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=5-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[5]</a></sup><li dir=ltr><span id=docs-internal-guid-7555fd7a-7fff-b63c-ab86-e8ef144a7390><strong>CPAP machines:</strong> If apnea persists or is severe, you may need a CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) machine, which provides a gentle flow of air to a mask that you’ll wear over your nose, keeping your airway open. Most people with sleep apnea find almost immediate relief with a CPAP machine, but some models can be unwieldy and uncomfortable.<span id=6-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#6 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#6>Cleveland Clinic</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>Oral Appliances for Sleep Apnea</span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=6-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[6]</a></sup> "I can tell a huge difference when I sleep with my CPAP machine versus without," says What to Expect Community mom Srhgranger. </span><li dir=ltr><strong>Sleep apnea patches</strong>: Other alternatives include sleep apnea patches, which allow air in but restrict the amount breathed out, forcing it back down the airways to keep them open. The patches might not be covered by your insurance plan, but the CPAP usually is. <li dir=ltr><strong>Oral appliances:</strong> A special mouthpiece — fitted by an experienced dentist — can also help keep your throat open by bringing your lower jaw forward or holding your tongue in a different position.</ul><h2 id=end>Does sleep apnea go away after pregnancy?</h2><p dir=ltr>Yes, there is some evidence that OSA in pregnancy will improve once you deliver. In fact, many studies indicate that sleep apnea gets better with weight loss, so once your sweet baby has arrived, your OSA symptoms should subside. <p dir=ltr>Weight loss alone, however, isn’t always a magic bullet for sleep apnea, and other approaches may be necessary. <p dir=ltr>Obstructive sleep apnea doesn’t have to ruin the quality sleep you need during pregnancy. If you keep track of the signs and symptoms of OSA and work with your doctor to treat the condition, you and your baby-to-be should be off to dreamland in no time.</p><br></div><div class="medical-authority py-4"><p>From the What to Expect editorial team and <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/about-heidi-murkoff/">Heidi Murkoff,</a> author of <em>What to Expect When You're Expecting</em>. 4 of pregnancy, your body is beginning to form the placenta and amniotic sac.<p>Symptoms like abdominal pressure and tender breasts may appear this week, and as the cluster of cells that will soon become your baby burrows into your uterine lining, you may also spot some <a class=waffle-rich-text-link href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/getting-pregnant/implantation-bleeding/">implantation bleeding</a>. (But if you don't notice any symptoms at all yet, that's completely normal too.)<p>Did you know you can track your daily symptoms and baby’s growth all in one place? Download the <a href=https://wte.onelink.me/85iI/7s0l3a5z rel="">What to Expect app</a> to get daily tips and weekly baby updates throughout your pregnancy.<section class=your-baby id=section-baby><h2 class=your-baby__headline>Your Baby at Week 4</h2><div class="jw-video-player-wrapper wbw-video wte-section" data-autostart=False data-placement=Media_tab data-playlist-id=AlwBOr2a data-play-ad=true><div id=jw-video-player--67989cebf6934a04b50d96c31943f2b8 class=jw-player></div><div class="wbw-video__info d-flex justify-content-center"><span id=video-title class="wbw-video__info__title text-center"></span></div></div><div class=your-baby__dev><div class=your-baby__dev__descr-c><h3 class=your-baby__dev__descr-c__headline>At a Glance</h3><div class=your-baby__dev__descr-c__items><div class=your-baby__dev__descr-c__items__item><div class=your-baby__dev__descr-c__items__item__img-c><img src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/pregnancy-week4-baby-development-image-a.svg class="rounded-circle your-baby__dev__descr-c__items__item__img-c__img" alt="Two sets of cells"></div><div class=your-baby__dev__descr-c__items__item__body-c><div class=your-baby__dev__descr-c__items__item__body-c__headline>Two sets of cells</div><div class=your-baby__dev__descr-c__items__item__body-c__body>Your itty bitty embryo has two layers of cells called the epiblast and the hypoblast. Soon they’ll develop into all of your baby’s body parts and systems.</div></div></div><div class=your-baby__dev__descr-c__items__item><div class=your-baby__dev__descr-c__items__item__img-c><img src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/pregnancy-week4-baby-development-image-b.svg class="rounded-circle your-baby__dev__descr-c__items__item__img-c__img" alt="Seeing double"></div><div class=your-baby__dev__descr-c__items__item__body-c><div class=your-baby__dev__descr-c__items__item__body-c__headline>Seeing double</div><div class=your-baby__dev__descr-c__items__item__body-c__body>You normally don't have your first ultrasound until at least week 6, but you might be able to spot the gestational sac as early as halfway through week 4 — and if you're having twins, you'll likely see two of them!</div></div></div><div class=your-baby__dev__descr-c__items__item><div class=your-baby__dev__descr-c__items__item__img-c><img src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/pregnancy-week4-baby-development-image-c.svg class="rounded-circle your-baby__dev__descr-c__items__item__img-c__img" alt="Baby's yolk sac"></div><div class=your-baby__dev__descr-c__items__item__body-c><div class=your-baby__dev__descr-c__items__item__body-c__headline>Baby's yolk sac</div><div class=your-baby__dev__descr-c__items__item__body-c__body>Before the placenta forms, you develop a yolk sac, which can be visible next week. This sac produces blood and helps to nourish your young embryo.</div></div></div></div></div></div><div id=lightbox-inline-form-a24547b8-5d55-4b23-971d-0c4672c8ffbb class=lightbox-inline-form-holder></div><div id=lightbox-inline-form-79fdff90-8a54-40e6-9db7-30b6ef1dd207 class=lightbox-inline-form-holder></div><div><h3><strong>4 weeks pregnant is how many months?</strong></h3><p>If you’re 4 weeks pregnant, you're in month 1 of your pregnancy. Only 8 months to go! Still have questions? Here's some more information on <a href=//www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/pregnancy-health/understanding-pregnancy-week.aspx>how weeks, months, and trimesters are broken down in pregnancy</a>.<h3>How big is my baby at 4 weeks?</h3><p>Despite its extremely tiny size — no longer than 1 millimeter and no bigger than a poppy seed (think about that as you eat your morning bagel) — your little embryo is busy setting up house. <h3>Placenta and embryo begin forming</h3><p>While you may have just started to wonder whether you're pregnant, your soon-to-be baby has already found its home: The blastocyst has completed its journey from your fallopian tube to your uterus.<p>Once there, it burrows into your uterine lining and <a href="/getting-pregnant/ovulation/implantation/" rel="">implants</a> — making that unbreakable connection to you that'll last the next eight months (and a lifetime after that).<p>As soon as that little ball of cells is settled in your uterus, it will undergo the great divide, splitting into two groups. Half of what's now called the embryo will become your son or daughter, while the other half forms <a href=//www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/placenta>the placenta</a>, your baby's lifeline — which channels nutrients and carries waste away until delivery.<h3>Development of the embryo and amniotic sac</h3><p>While the amniotic sac (also called the bag of waters) forms around it, so does the yolk sac, which will later be incorporated into <a href="//www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/fetal-development/fetal-digestive-system/">your baby's developing digestive tract</a>.<p>The embryo now has three distinct layers of cells that will grow into specialized parts of your baby's body. The inner layer, known as the endoderm, will develop into your baby's digestive system, liver, and lungs. The middle layer, called the mesoderm, will soon be your baby's heart, sex organs, bones, kidneys, and muscles. And the outer layer, or ectoderm, will eventually form your baby's nervous system, hair, eyes, and outer layer of skin.</div></section><section class="your-body wte-section wte-section-border-bottom" id=section-body><h2 class=your-body__headline>Your Body at Week 4</h2><div class=your-body__img-c><img src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms//redesign/lazy-load-img-placeholder.svg data-src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/wbw-body-t10-2021-722x406-week-05.jpg alt="baby size at 4 weeks pregnant" class="your-body__img-c__img __lazy-load" data-srcset="//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/wbw-body-t10-2021-722x406-week-05.jpg?width=80 80w, //images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/wbw-body-t10-2021-722x406-week-05.jpg?width=150 150w, //images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/wbw-body-t10-2021-722x406-week-05.jpg?width=300 300w, //images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/wbw-body-t10-2021-722x406-week-05.jpg?width=396 396w, //images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/wbw-body-t10-2021-722x406-week-05.jpg?width=650 650w, //images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/wbw-body-t10-2021-722x406-week-05.jpg?width=850 850w, //images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/wbw-body-t10-2021-722x406-week-05.jpg?width=1200 1200w" sizes="(min-width: 1300px) 374px, (min-width: 727px) 374px, 100vw"></div><div class=your-body__body><h3>No symptoms yet?</h3><p>Just a week after fertilization, baby-making is still in its infancy, so to speak. At 4 weeks pregnant, your body is gearing up, big-time — transforming quickly into a baby-growing haven that will house your little miracle for the next nine months or so.<p>Chances are you're oblivious to all the hubbub. While some women experience those pesky, PMS-like <a class=page-links href="/pregnancy/symptoms-and-solutions/early-signs-of-pregnancy-before-missed-period/">early pregnancy symptoms</a>, including mood swings, bloating, and <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/symptoms-and-solutions/abdominal-cramps.aspx>cramping</a>, others don't feel a thing.<p>Whatever you're feeling or not feeling, it may be too early to see a reliable result on your <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/getting-pregnant/fertility/putting-home-pregnancy-tests-to-the-test.aspx rel="">pregnancy test</a>.<h3>The egg implants</h3><p>Though you may not feel pregnant quite yet, here's what's going on behind the scenes.<p>The fertilized egg and your uterus are making contact this week in <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/getting-pregnant/ovulation/implantation/">a process called implantation</a>, as the blastocyst you'll one day call your baby begins to attach itself to the uterine lining.<p>Up to 25% of the time, <a href="/getting-pregnant/implantation-bleeding/" rel="">implantation bleeding</a> will occur as that bundle of cells burrows its way into the uterine wall. Implantation bleeding, which is usually very scant and either light pink, light red, or light brown, occurs earlier than your expected period. <p>Don't mistake it for your period and don't worry about the bleeding — it's not a sign that something is wrong. You might feel a little pressure in your abdomen (nothing to worry about!) and your breasts may feel a little tender and become even bigger (but get ready for more growth spurts!).<h3>Pregnancy hormones will soon make an appearance</h3><p>Within six to 12 days after fertilization, the egg starts to release <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/ask-heidi/hcg-levels.aspx>hCG, or human chorionic gonadotropin</a> — the pregnancy hormone that will very soon turn that line on your pregnancy test pink or blue and your world upside down.<p>HCG alerts the corpus luteum (the once-follicle this egg was released from) that it needs to stick around and produce progesterone and estrogen to nourish the pregnancy until the placenta takes over about eight weeks from now.</div></section><section class="wbw-symptoms wte-section-border-bottom" id=section-symptoms><div class=wbw-symptoms__headline><h2>Pregnancy Symptoms Week 4</h2></div><div class=wbw-symptoms__list><div class=container><div class="row no-gutters"><div class=wbw-symptoms__list__item__img-c><img src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms//redesign/lazy-load-img-placeholder.svg data-src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/pregnancy-wbw-w4-implantation-bleeding-315x315.jpg class="rounded-circle wbw-symptoms__list__item__img-c__img __lazy-load" alt="Implantation bleeding"></div><div class=wbw-symptoms__list__item__body-c__headline><a href="/getting-pregnant/implantation-bleeding/" class="wbw-symptoms__list__item__body-c__headline__link wte-no-reset"> Implantation bleeding </a><div class="wbw-symptoms__list__item__body-c__body hide" id=wbw-symptoms__list__item__1 style=display:none>If you find that you’re spotting this week — around the time you would have had your period — don’t worry. It's usually a sign that the embryo has implanted itself into the uterine wall. Don’t have any spotting at all? All good too, as less than 25% of women experience implantation bleeding. <a href="/getting-pregnant/implantation-bleeding/" class="wbw-symptoms__list__item__body-c__body__readmore wte-no-reset">Read class="wbw-tips__list wbw-tips__list"><div class="wbw-tips__list__item wbw-tips__list__item"><div class="wbw-tips__list__item__body-c wbw-tips__list__item__body-c"><div class="wbw-tips__list__item__body-c__headline wbw-tips__list__item__body-c__headline"><strong>Take a prenatal vitamin</strong></div><div class="wbw-tips__list__item__body-c__body show" id=wbw-tips__list__item__1><p dir=ltr><span>If you haven’t started taking a </span><a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/baby-products/pregnancy/best-prenatal-vitamins-buy-over-counter/"><span>prenatal vitamin</span></a><span> yet, now’s the time. (And no, a standard multi won’t do.) Prenatals contain vitamins and minerals that are essential for your growing baby.</span><p dir=ltr><span>For example, folic acid (aka folate) — which is found naturally in whole grains, green leafy vegetables, beans, bananas, broccoli, and milk, and added via fortification to breads and cereals — is not only critical for neural tube development early in pregnancy but also for the development of your </span><a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/fetal-development/fetal-brain-nervous-system/"><span>baby's brain</span></a><span> during all nine months.</span><p dir=ltr><span>The best prenatal for you is the one that you can actually tolerate — which, for some people, may be a chewable or liquid option, or a softgel coated in gelatin.</span><p dir=ltr><span>Whichever prenatal you choose, make sure it hits, or comes close to, the recommended intake of folic acid, iron (if you can tolerate it), calcium, vitamin D, choline, omega-3 fatty acids, B vitamins, and vitamin C.</span></div></div></div><div class="wbw-tips__list__item wbw-tips__list__item"><div class="wbw-tips__list__item__body-c wbw-tips__list__item__body-c"><div class="wbw-tips__list__item__body-c__headline wbw-tips__list__item__body-c__headline"><strong>Find your due date</strong></div><div class="wbw-tips__list__item__body-c__body show" id=wbw-tips__list__item__2><p dir=ltr><span>Think you need a Ph.D. in quantum physics to figure out your </span><a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/due-date-calculator/"><span>due date</span></a><span>? Doing the math is actually a lot easier than you think — even if you slept through high school algebra. Your estimated due date is 40 weeks from the first day of your last period.</span><p dir=ltr><span>Here's the slightly confusing part: If you do give birth on that day, your baby will have clocked in only 38 weeks in utero, not 40. That's because the pregnancy countdown begins two weeks before your baby is even conceived — making you about four weeks pregnant before you see a positive pregnancy test.</span><p dir=ltr><span>Regardless, you shouldn't plan your schedule around your estimated due date. After all, it is just an estimate. Most babies are born between 38 and 42 weeks, and babies of first-time moms are more likely to arrive on the later side. Only a handful of babies actually make their debuts right on schedule.</span></div></div></div><div class="wbw-tips__list__item wbw-tips__list__item"><div class="wbw-tips__list__item__body-c wbw-tips__list__item__body-c"><div class="wbw-tips__list__item__body-c__headline wbw-tips__list__item__body-c__headline"><strong>Does a faint line mean you’re pregnant?</strong></div><div class="wbw-tips__list__item__body-c__body show" id=wbw-tips__list__item__3><p dir=ltr><span>If your pregnant test is showing a barely visible, </span><a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/getting-pregnant/prepping-for-pregnancy/faint-line-pregnancy-test/"><span>faint line</span></a><span> — one that looks more like a smudge of chalk — it usually means that implantation has occurred. </span><p dir=ltr><span>Still, you’ll want to take the test again in a few days or so to make sure the line has become thicker and darker, which means your pregnancy is progressing.</span><p><span id=docs-internal-guid-5697c07c-7fff-e9c1-4814-6d9b8342ba31><span>If you see a faint line on your pregnancy test but get your period later on, that means you were only briefly pregnant. In this case, you may have experienced a very early (and common) pregnancy loss called a </span><a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/chemical-pregnancy/"><span>chemical pregnancy</span></a><span>. As upsetting as this may be, it won’t impact your ability to get pregnant in the future.</span></span></div></div></div><div class="wbw-tips__list__item wbw-tips__list__item"><div class="wbw-tips__list__item__body-c wbw-tips__list__item__body-c"><div class="wbw-tips__list__item__body-c__headline wbw-tips__list__item__body-c__headline"><strong>Can you choose the sex of your baby?</strong></div><div class="wbw-tips__list__item__body-c__body show" id=wbw-tips__list__item__4><p dir=ltr><span>Priority number one is having a healthy baby. But it’s not uncommon to have your heart set on having a boy or girl, especially if you’ve already had a baby of the opposite sex. </span><p dir=ltr><span>Unless you’re getting an assist from science — in the form of preimplantation genetic diagnosis (which is used along with IVF) or sperm sorting — there’s no real way to </span><a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/getting-pregnant/ask-heidi/gender-selection.aspx><span>choose the sex of your baby</span></a><span>. </span><p dir=ltr><span>That said, some couples swear by the Shettles Method, which theorizes that having sex as close to ovulation as possible can net you a baby boy (Y-sperm are supposedly speedier); having sex two to three days before ovulation can yield a baby girl (X-sperm are supposedly slower but more resilient).</span></div></div></div><div class="wbw-tips__list__item wbw-tips__list__item"><div class="wbw-tips__list__item__body-c wbw-tips__list__item__body-c"><div class="wbw-tips__list__item__body-c__headline wbw-tips__list__item__body-c__headline"><strong>Here’s how long it takes to get pregnant</strong></div><div class="wbw-tips__list__item__body-c__body show" id=wbw-tips__list__item__5><p dir=ltr><span>In general, healthy couples have a 20 to 25% </span><a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/getting-pregnant/fertility/how-long-does-it-take-to-get-pregnant><span>chance of getting pregnant</span></a><span> during each month’s cycle. The catch: That assumes you’re having sex “regularly” — two to three times a week — and without contraception. About 85% of couples who are trying to conceive will get pregnant within a year.</span><p dir=ltr><span>Once sperm meets egg, you can expect the process to go fairly quickly — it’ll take about two to three weeks for the fertilized egg to travel to the uterus and implant on the uterine wall, resulting in a pregnancy.</span></div></div></div><div class="wbw-tips__list__item wbw-tips__list__item"><div class="wbw-tips__list__item__body-c wbw-tips__list__item__body-c"><div class="wbw-tips__list__item__body-c__headline wbw-tips__list__item__body-c__headline"><strong>Know the symptoms of implantation</strong></div><div class="wbw-tips__list__item__body-c__body show" id=wbw-tips__list__item__6><p dir=ltr><span>Once the </span><a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/getting-pregnant/fertility/how-fertilization-happens.aspx><span>fertilized egg</span></a><span> travels down the fallopian tubes, it will implant into the wall of the uterus — a process aptly known as </span><a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/getting-pregnant/ovulation/implantation/"><span>implantation</span></a><span>. Many women don’t experience any symptoms of implantation, but some will feel abdominal cramps and </span><a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/getting-pregnant/implantation-bleeding/"><span>light bleeding</span></a><span>.</span><p dir=ltr><span>Whether you feel anything or not, implantation marks the beginning of your pregnancy. It won’t be long now!</span></div></div></div><div class="wbw-tips__list__item wbw-tips__list__item"><div class="wbw-tips__list__item__body-c wbw-tips__list__item__body-c"><div class="wbw-tips__list__item__body-c__headline wbw-tips__list__item__body-c__headline"><strong>Skip the DIY pregnancy tests</strong></div><div class="wbw-tips__list__item__body-c__body show" id=wbw-tips__list__item__7><p dir=ltr><a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy-products/pregnancy/best-pregnancy-test/"><span>Drugstore pregnancy tests</span></a><span> aren’t always cheap, but they </span><span>are</span><span> up to 99% accurate. Homemade pregnancy tests, on the other hand — while popular with bloggers and on YouTube — aren’t reliable at all (though they can be entertaining to try!).</span><p><span id=docs-internal-guid-9338fe3b-7fff-c951-7c8c-2c3940d363e1><span>The thinking goes that by combining your urine with </span><a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/getting-pregnant/prepping-for-pregnancy/pregnancy-test-with-salt/"><span>salt</span></a><span>, </span><a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/getting-pregnant/prepping-for-pregnancy/sugar-pregnancy-test/"><span>sugar</span></a><span>, <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/getting-pregnant/prepping-for-pregnancy/toothpaste-pregnancy-test/" rel="">toothpaste</a>, or even </span><a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/getting-pregnant/prepping-for-pregnancy/homemade-bleach-pregnancy-test/"><span>bleach</span></a><span>, you can detect the presence of the pregnancy hormone <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/ask-heidi/hcg-levels.aspx rel="">human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)</a>. </span></span><p><span id=docs-internal-guid-9338fe3b-7fff-c951-7c8c-2c3940d363e1><span>But there’s no evidence that these tests can yield an accurate result, and no major medical organization recommends using them. Still, if you want to try one for fun, have at it (as long as you go in knowing they're just for laughs).</span></span></div></div></div></div></section><div class=medical-authority><div class=medical-authority__reviewDate><a class=medical-authority__reviewDate__link href="/medical-review/"> <img src="data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAD/ACwAAAAAAQABAAACADs=" data-src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms//redesign/gray-tick.png class="__lazy-load medical-authority__tick" alt="Medical Reviewed"> Reviewed July 29, 2025 </a></div><p>From the What to Expect editorial team and <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/about-heidi-murkoff/">Heidi Murkoff,</a> author of <em>What to Expect When You're Expecting</em>.
