xlink:href=#bottom-arrow /></svg></div></div></div></div></div><div class=article-body><p><strong>A pregnant woman's “water breaking” refers to the rupture of the amniotic sac (or membranes), resulting in leaking fluid that’s typically clear and odorless. This is a signal that your baby is almost ready to be born, and most moms-to-be experience their water breaking during or at the beginning of labor. If the fluid is green or brown, it warrants an immediate call to your doctor. <br></strong><p><span id=docs-internal-guid-aaaa12ba-7fff-06f5-7643-4288bb7547b7>By now, you may be wondering when — and at what inconvenient place — your water will break. Most women will have their water break during the early <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/labor-and-delivery/childbirth-stages/three-phases-of-labor.aspx rel="">stages of labor</a> — and it's usually a much less dramatic event than you may have been led to believe.</span><div id=WhatToExpect_Slideshow data-primis-ad style=margin-top:20px;margin-bottom:20px><script>(function(){function loadPrimis(){var s=document.createElement("script");s.type="text/javascript";s.src="https://live.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?s=121100&cbuster=1782858570989&playerApiId=WhatToExpect_Slideshow";document.getElementById("WhatToExpect_Slideshow").appendChild(s);}
if(window.WTEAdInfo){loadPrimis();}else{window.addEventListener("WTEAdInfoReady",loadPrimis,{once:true});}})();</script></div><p><section class=keytakeaways-c><div class=keytakeaways-c__header><div class=keytakeaways-c__header__summary-icon><img src=https://images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/redesign/key_takeaways.svg alt="summary icon" width=24 height=24></div><div class=keytakeaways-c__header__title>Key Takeaways</div></div><div class=keytakeaways-c__body><ul><li><strong>Your "water breaking" is the rupture of the amniotic sac. </strong>Amniotic fluid is typically clear or pale yellow with a sweet smell; if it looks green or brown, or if rupture occurs before 37 weeks, contact your doctor immediately.<li><strong>For most pregnant women, their water breaks during active labor</strong> — only about 1 in 10 moms-to-be experience it beforehand, and many require artificial rupture by a practitioner.<li><strong>If your water breaks without contractions, </strong>labor usually follows within 12 to 24 hours. But to reduce infection risk, most practitioners will induce within 24 hours if contractions don't start naturally.</ul></div></section><h2 id=signs>How can you tell if your water breaks?</h2><p dir=ltr>It’s hard to say exactly how much fluid you’ll lose when your water breaks. It may feel like stream of warm liquid that makes your underwear and possibly even your pants wet. But more likely is that it will be a slow and steady trickle of fluid.<span id=1-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#1 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#1>Mayo Clinic</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>Water Breaking: Understand This Sign of Labor</span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=1-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[1]</a></sup> <p dir=ltr>"I was pushing at the hospital and felt a warm gush, I stopped pushing and yelled, 'Did I just pee?!' My doctor laughed and said, 'No, your water just broke!'" recalls <a href="https://community.whattoexpect.com/forums/" rel="">What to Expect Community</a> mom HC07.<p dir=ltr>Community mom mcdonohue had a different experience: "With my first, my water popped quiet dramatically, a huge gush and it looked like I peed my pants while we were out to lunch with my husband's coworkers. With my second, my water broke at home while I was feeding my toddler lunch. It was a small trickle instead of the big gush."<p dir=ltr>Once your water breaks, you may notice a continuous drip of clear or pale yellow and odorless or sweet-smelling amniotic fluid that won’t let up until your baby is born. You’ll want to wear a pad until you can get to the hospital or birthing center (or bring a towel and a change of underwear).<p dir=ltr>If you’re not sure whether your water broke, call your doctor or head to your place of delivery as soon as possible so they can verify whether you’re actually leaking amniotic fluid.<h2 id=cause>What causes your water to break?</h2><p dir=ltr><span id=docs-internal-guid-6a069610-7fff-213f-474d-43e101906f01>No one knows for sure what triggers the chemical chain reaction that <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/labor-and-delivery/">begins labor</a> — typically around <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/week-by-week/week-40.aspx rel="">week 40 of pregnancy</a> — but experts point to a number of complicated factors, including brain signals from the fetus.</span><h2 id=discharge>Is it my water breaking or is it discharge?</h2><p dir=ltr>Amniotic fluid is a pale, straw-colored fluid. <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/symptoms-and-solutions/vaginal-discharge.aspx>Vaginal discharge</a>, on the other hand, is a thin, milky-white mucus that’s similar to but heavier than what you might experience between periods.<p dir=ltr>Your water breaking may be accompanied by bloody show. This mucusy discharge is streaked pink or brown with blood, and it’s a sign that labor is imminent. <p dir=ltr>You might also <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/symptoms-and-solutions/mucous-plug.aspx>lose your mucus plug</a>, which looks like you probably imagine: a glob of mucus. It’s usually a <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/labor-signs>sign that labor is near</a> (though some women can lose it weeks before delivery), but you may not notice it at all.<p><div class=jw-video-player-wrapper data-video-id=FgYYvFTb data-placement=Inline><div id=jw-video-player-FgYYvFTb class=jw-player></div></div><div class="wbw-video__info d-flex justify-content-center mb-3"><span class="wbw-video__info__title text-center"></span></div><h2 id=pee>Is it pee or did my water break?</h2><p dir=ltr>Though many pregnant women leak urine, especially in the <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/third-trimester-of-pregnancy.aspx>third trimester</a>, a sniff will probably clue you in. If the fluid is yellowish and smells of ammonia, it's probably urine. If it doesn’t smell or smells sort of sweet, it’s probably amniotic fluid.<h2 id=labor>Will my water break before I go into labor?</h2><p dir=ltr>Don't worry too much about your water breaking when you're in the checkout line: Only about 1 in 10 women experience the rupture of the amniotic sac before they go into labor, <a href=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/jmwh.12509 target=_blank rel="">according to the <em>Journal of Midwifery and Women's Health</em></a>. That means that for the other 90% of women, their water will break once they’re already having contractions.<span id=2-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#2 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#2>Journal of Midwifery & Women%u2019s Health</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>Ruptured Membranes: When the Bag of Water Breaks</span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=2-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[2]</a></sup><p dir=ltr><span id=docs-internal-guid-ed7ed7f8-7fff-927d-570f-5f6516d9d9b6>So chances are good that you'll have plenty of warning or you'll already be in the hospital when your water breaks. And lots of women require the <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/labor-and-delivery/procedures-and-interventions/artificial-rupture-of-membranes.aspx>artificial rupture of the membranes</a> by their practitioner, called an amniotomy.</span><h2 id=contractions>What if my water breaks but I don’t have any contractions?</h2><p dir=ltr>It’s likely that labor’s on the way, and soon. Most women whose membranes rupture before labor begins can expect to <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/symptoms-and-solutions/labor-contractions.aspx>feel the first contractions</a> within 12 hours of that initial trickle, while others can expect them to start within 24 hours. In the meantime, you won't run out of amniotic fluid — your body continues to produce it right up until delivery.<p dir=ltr>For some moms, however, labor takes a little longer to get going. To prevent infection through the ruptured amniotic sac (the longer it takes for labor to get going, the greater the risk), most practitioners <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/labor-induction/">induce labor</a> within 24 hours of a rupture if you’re near your due date; some induce as early as six hours after.<h2 id=do>What should you do if your water breaks?</h2><p dir=ltr>Your health care provider has probably given you a set of instructions to follow when your water breaks. Follow them. If you don't remember the instructions or have any doubts about how to proceed, call your practitioner night or day.<p dir=ltr>If your instructions are to wait for contractions over the next 12 hours or so, you'll need to guard yourself and your baby against infection now that the protective barrier of the amniotic sac has been breached. Use panty liners or maxi pads, not tampons, to keep the amniotic fluid from wetting your clothes, and keep your vaginal area clean. When you go to the bathroom, be especially careful to wipe from front to back. And not that you're likely in the mood, but sex is now officially off-limits.<p dir=ltr>If you tested positive for <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/pregnancy-health/prenatal-testing-group-b-strep/">group B strep</a> in the weeks leading up to your due date, your practitioner will tell you that you need to get to the hospital right away after your water breaks (if it happens before you have contractions and go into labor), since there is a risk of infection.<span id=3-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#3 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#3>American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>Group B Strep and Pregnancy</span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=3-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[3]</a></sup><h2 id=early>What happens if your water breaks early?</h2><p dir=ltr>If your water breaks after <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/week-by-week/week-37.aspx rel="">week 37 of pregnancy</a> but before you’re in labor, it’s known as prelabor rupture of the membranes. Labor will likely begin on its own within 12 hours. If it doesn’t, your doctor will induce labor soon to reduce the infection risk.<span id=4-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#4 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#4>American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>Prelabor Rupture of Membranes</span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=4-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[4]</a></sup><p dir=ltr><span id=docs-internal-guid-d8c77b79-7fff-2d91-0bd0-b0e9fb4fb77a>If your water ruptures before week 37 of pregnancy, it’s known as <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/pregnancy-health/complications/preterm-rupture-of-membranes.aspx>preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM)</a>. </span>You may have an increased risk of PPROM if you:<ul><li dir=ltr><a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/pregnancy-health/smoking-cigarettes-during-pregnancy/" rel="">Smoke during pregnancy</a><li dir=ltr>Have experienced <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/symptoms-and-solutions/vaginal-spotting.aspx rel="">vaginal bleeding</a> during the second and third trimesters<li dir=ltr>Had an early membrane rupture in the past<li dir=ltr>Have bacterial vaginosis <li dir=ltr>Are <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/twins-and-multiples/" rel="">carrying multiples</a></ul><p><span id=docs-internal-guid-a0471fdc-7fff-9f63-ac3d-590e372f94c6>If your water does break before 37 weeks, call your doctor immediately. PPROM may require hospitalization or delivery and comes with the <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/preterm-labor/">risk of preterm labor</a>, infection of the amniotic fluid, <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/pregnancy-health/complications/placental-abruption.aspx>placental abruption</a>, and umbilical cord prolapse.</span><h2 id=doctor>Should you call the doctor if your water breaks?</h2><p>Wondering when it's time to call your practitioner ASAP? Follow these guidelines:<ul><li>Your water breaks and the fluid looks green or brown, which may mean your baby had a bowel movement in utero (known as <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/health-and-safety/newborn-infant-baby-poop/" rel="">meconium</a>).<li>You're at 37 weeks or earlier in your pregnancy (though it's unlikely this will happen).<li>Your water breaks and your <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/breech-baby/">baby is in a breech position</a>. Breech babies have a higher risk of complications during delivery, so you’ll likely need a C-section.<li>You experience a small, one-time gush of fluid. It's possible the membrane has ruptured, but your baby's head came down and stopped the leak. This ups the risk of infection.<li>You feel something in your vagina or see a loop of the umbilical cord at the vaginal opening. Call 911. Rarely, when the membranes rupture before labor begins and the baby’s not yet engaged in the pelvis (more likely when the baby is breech or preterm), the <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/pregnancy-health/complications/cord-prolapse.aspx>umbilical cord can become “prolapsed”</a> — swept into the cervix or even the vagina with the trickle of amniotic fluid.</ul><p><span id=docs-internal-guid-97cf2a73-7fff-865f-3ea3-6ed05efe9b47>Chances are, your water will break right on time — think: when you’re already in the hospital, not halfway through dinner at a fancy restaurant. In fact, some women don’t notice their water breaking at all. Whenever your water breaks (or even if it doesn't before you're in the hospital), just know that it won’t be much longer before your little one arrives.</span></p><br></div><div class="medical-authority py-4"><p>From the What to Expect editorial team and <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/about-heidi-murkoff/">Heidi Murkoff,</a> author of <em>What to Expect When You're Expecting</em>. risks?</div></a></ul></div></div></div></div><div class=article-body><p><strong>Ultrasounds use soundwaves to monitor fetal development. These scans confirm your due date, monitor your little one's growth, and check for complications. Experts recommend at least one between weeks 18 and 22, with a possible additional first trimester ultrasound as well, though the exact number moms-to-be get can vary.</strong><p>Between the <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/morning-sickness/" rel="">nausea</a>, <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/symptoms-and-solutions/cravings-and-aversions.aspx rel="">cravings</a>, and <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/symptoms-and-solutions/frequent-urination.aspx rel="">constant need to pee</a>, you know something’s going on in there. But pregnancy sometimes doesn’t feel entirely real until you have that first peek at your baby during your <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/pregnancy-health/first-prenatal-appointment/" rel="">first prenatal</a> ultrasound. Fortunately, pregnancy ultrasounds are a very standard — and very welcome — part of prenatal care. Here's what to know.<div id=WhatToExpect_Slideshow data-primis-ad style=margin-top:20px;margin-bottom:20px><script>(function(){function loadPrimis(){var s=document.createElement("script");s.type="text/javascript";s.src="https://live.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?s=121100&cbuster=1782858573438&playerApiId=WhatToExpect_Slideshow";document.getElementById("WhatToExpect_Slideshow").appendChild(s);}
if(window.WTEAdInfo){loadPrimis();}else{window.addEventListener("WTEAdInfoReady",loadPrimis,{once:true});}})();</script></div><p><section class=keytakeaways-c><div class=keytakeaways-c__header><div class=keytakeaways-c__header__summary-icon><img src=https://images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/redesign/key_takeaways.svg alt="summary icon" width=24 height=24></div><div class=keytakeaways-c__header__title>Key Takeaways</div></div><div class=keytakeaways-c__body><ul><li><strong>You'll likely have at least one ultrasound during your pregnancy. </strong>Experts recommend at least one between weeks 18 and 22, though most moms-to-be also have one in the first trimester. Your practitioner might suggest additional scans depending on any risk factors or complications.<li><strong>There are two main types of ultrasounds </strong>— transvaginal (used earlier in pregnancy) and transabdominal — both are painless and last around 20 minutes.<li><strong>Experts advise against keepsake 3D or 4D ultrasounds from private companies </strong>as well as at-home fetal monitors, and recommend limiting scans to one or two unless medically necessary.</ul></div></section><h2 id=what>What is an ultrasound?</h2><p dir=ltr>An ultrasound is a type of imaging technology that uses soundwaves to create a picture, or sonogram, of structures inside your body, including your growing baby. During pregnancy, a transducer or wand is placed in your vagina or on top of your belly. The wand emits soundwaves that bounce off your baby’s tissues, fluids, and bones and translates them into the image of your baby that you see on the screen.<p dir=ltr><span id=docs-internal-guid-712c6eff-7fff-b4ba-65f5-4e7d0caa582b>Early in pregnancy, ultrasounds are used to confirm the fetal heartbeat and the baby’s position in your uterus. Later, ultrasounds screen for fetal growth and placenta location, as well as baby's general health and anatomy. </span><p dir=ltr><span id=docs-internal-guid-1b996092-7fff-62d1-cd6a-e539fa200052>Toward the end of pregnancy, ultrasounds can be used to check the length of your cervix (especially if there is any suspicion that you may be in preterm labor) as well as verifying that your baby is in a head-down position before delivery.</span><h2 id=when>When are ultrasounds done during pregnancy?</h2><p dir=ltr>The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) says that <a href=https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/ultrasound-exams target=_blank rel="">women should get at least one sonogram in the second trimester</a>, between weeks 18 and 22 of pregnancy.<span id=1-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#1 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#1>American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>Ultrasound Exams</span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=1-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[1]</a></sup> You may also receive an additional ultrasound in the <a href=/first-trimester-of-pregnancy.aspx rel="">first trimester</a>, before your 14th week of pregnancy. <p dir=ltr><span id=docs-internal-guid-cf90183c-7fff-77cd-a5f6-d9dc95c348eb>However, if you have certain chronic conditions such as <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/asthma-during-pregnancy rel="">asthma</a> or obesity, the timing of your ultrasounds may vary.</span><h3 dir=ltr>First-trimester ultrasound</h3><p dir=ltr>An early ultrasound is often a routine part of prenatal care between 6 and 9 weeks of pregnancy, though it can happen anytime before week 14. But a first-trimester ultrasound isn’t standard practice because it’s still too early for your practitioner to see your baby in detail. <p dir=ltr>Most practitioners wait until at least 6 weeks to perform the first pregnancy ultrasound. However, a gestational sac can be seen as early as 4 1/2 weeks after your last period, and a fetal heartbeat can be detected at 5 to 6 weeks (though that isn’t always the case). <span id=docs-internal-guid-30180349-7fff-a131-88a1-fc3259b1398a>The gestational sac provides nourishment and eventually produces cells that turn into baby’s umbilical cord, blood cells, and reproductive organs.</span><p dir=ltr><span id=docs-internal-guid-78c80f5c-7fff-e97b-8bbb-528ad5bacedd>If your doctor decides to perform an early ultrasound, it gives you a welcome first glance of your baby. This sneak peek is used to:<span id=2-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#2 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#2>National Institutes of Health, National Library of Medicine, Medline Plus</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>Ultrasound</span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=2-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[2]</a></sup></span><ul><li dir=ltr>Confirm <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/due-date-calculator/">your estimated due date</a> more accurately by measuring the fetus <li dir=ltr>Check the <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/fetal-development/fetal-heart-heartbeat-circulatory-system/">fetal heartbeat</a><li dir=ltr>Make sure the pregnancy is in the uterus <span id=docs-internal-guid-1859a7f5-7fff-dcf2-f899-1aa65410d8de>(to rule out an <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/ectopic-pregnancy/">ectopic pregnancy</a>, which typically happens in a fallopian tube)</span><li dir=ltr>Determine whether you’re carrying multiples </ul><p><div class=jw-video-player-wrapper data-video-id=XPfH88yX data-placement=Inline><div id=jw-video-player-XPfH88yX class=jw-player></div></div><div class="wbw-video__info d-flex justify-content-center mb-3"><span class="wbw-video__info__title text-center"></span></div><h3 id=docs-internal-guid-1a8ba3a8-7fff-b836-8403-9ec7811c864d dir=ltr>Second-trimester ultrasound</h3><p dir=ltr><span id=docs-internal-guid-5a7d4f4a-7fff-b2bf-7095-cc463c697270>Midway through your pregnancy, between weeks 18 and week 22, a <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/pregnancy-health/prenatal-testing-level-two-ultrasound-anatomy-scan/">level 2 ultrasound</a> will be done to see baby’s anatomy in detail. </span><p dir=ltr>The <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/screenings-and-tests/20-week-ultrasound-tips rel="">second-trimester ultrasound</a> is reassuring and fun to watch. It also offers you and your practitioner a picture of the overall health of your baby and your pregnancy by:<ul><li dir=ltr>Measuring your baby’s size and checking all major organs<li dir=ltr>Estimating the amount of amniotic fluid in your uterus to make sure the level is normal <li dir=ltr>Verifying the position of the placenta<li dir=ltr>Telling you your baby's sex (if you want to know)<li dir=ltr><span id=docs-internal-guid-41b88970-7fff-4a3e-6b7a-3438245c1c9c>Giving you a glimpse of your baby's hands, feet, and face</span></ul><p>Routine second trimester ultrasounds are usually done in 2D. Most practitioners reserve the <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/pregnancy-health/prenatal-testing-3d-4d-ultrasounds/">more detailed 3D and 4D ultrasounds</a> for when they’re medically necessary to more closely examine a fetus for a suspected anomaly.<h3 dir=ltr>Additional ultrasounds during pregnancy</h3><p dir=ltr>There are several reasons you may have additional ultrasounds during your pregnancy, including if:<ul><li dir=ltr>You have any <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/symptoms-and-solutions/vaginal-spotting.aspx>spotting during pregnancy</a>, to confirm that all is well<li dir=ltr>You’re carrying multiples, to monitor their growth<li dir=ltr>You’re <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/preterm-labor/">at risk of preterm labor</a>, to check for changes in the cervix<li dir=ltr>Your practitioner wants to check whether your baby may be too large to deliver vaginally (for example, you have a very small pelvis or your practitioner suspects your baby is very large)<li dir=ltr>Your practitioner wants to verify if your baby is in a head-down position before birth</ul><p dir=ltr>Additionally, ultrasounds are a part of several other pregnancy tests, including:<ul><li dir=ltr><a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/pregnancy-health/prenatal-testing-chorionic-villus-sampling/">Chorionic villus sampling (CVS)</a><li dir=ltr><a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/pregnancy-health/prenatal-testing-amniocentesis/">Amniocentesis</a><li dir=ltr><a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/pregnancy-health/prenatal-testing-nuchal-translucency-screening/">Nuchal translucency screening</a> <li dir=ltr><a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/pregnancy-health/prenatal-testing-biophysical-profile/">Biophysical profiles</a></ul><p dir=ltr>Doctors sometimes recommend a fetal echocardiogram, or a detailed ultrasound of a baby’s heart that’s performed by a trained technician and analyzed by a pediatric cardiologist. Your practitioner may suggest an echocardiogram if you have certain risk factors, including:<ul><li dir=ltr>You have a family history of congenital heart defects <li dir=ltr>Your baby’s been diagnosed with a genetic condition (like Down syndrome) <li dir=ltr>You had abnormal results during another pregnancy test<li dir=ltr>You have certain health conditions (like diabetes or an autoimmune disease) <li dir=ltr>Your baby has an abnormal heart rhythm or rate<li dir=ltr>You had certain infections during pregnancy, including rubella or <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/pregnancy-health/complications/cytomegalovirus.aspx rel="">cytomegalovirus (CMV)</a></ul><p>"My doc does two [ultrasounds], one at 8 weeks and the anatomy scan at 20 weeks. That's it. She said they don't do any more than that unless there are complications or concerns," says <a href="https://community.whattoexpect.com/forums/" rel="">What to Expect Community</a> mom Badwolf24.<p>"I have had one [ultrasound] at 8 weeks and 13 weeks, and have the anatomy scan scheduled for 20 weeks and a final check at 36 weeks," says Community mom Expectingababy. "The 13-week scan was 'just for fun,' according to the OB. I wasn't going to argue!" <h2 id=prepare>How can you prepare for your pregnancy ultrasound?</h2><p dir=ltr><span id=docs-internal-guid-f2b3427c-7fff-3523-d2d8-d58448391d3c>If your doctor orders a transabdominal ultrasound, you should arrive at your appointment with a full bladder. This makes it easier for your doctor or sonographer to see around or through your bladder.</span><p dir=ltr>To time it right, some practitioners suggest emptying your bladder about 90 minutes before your exam. Then drink an 8-ounce beverage of your choice (water, juice, and milk are all fine) about an hour before your appointment.<span id=3-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#3 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#3>March of Dimes</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>Ultrasound During Pregnancy</span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=3-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[3]</a></sup><p dir=ltr>Eating about an hour before your appointment — especially something sugary — will also get your baby moving around. This can help the sonographer take better pictures. <p dir=ltr>Otherwise, there are no other specific preparations required for a pregnancy ultrasound. Your job: Sit back and enjoy the show!<h2 id=expect>What should you expect during the first pregnancy ultrasound?</h2><p><span id=docs-internal-guid-bec6501c-7fff-f07b-cb0a-4020f05f0258>There are two main types of ultrasounds used during pregnancy: transvaginal and transabdominal ultrasounds. Both types of scans are painless and typically last about 20 minutes. The type you have will depend on how far along you are in your pregnancy.<span id=4-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#4 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#4>National Institutes of Health, MedlinePlus</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>Ultrasound</span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=4-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[4]</a></sup> </span><p>During your first ultrasound, you'll be able to watch along with your practitioner (though you'll probably need help understanding what you're seeing). You’ll likely even take home a small printout as a souvenir.<h3 dir=ltr>Transvaginal ultrasound</h3><p dir=ltr>If you're getting your first pregnancy ultrasound before week 6 or 7, your practitioner will likely perform a transvaginal ultrasound. A small, long transducer (or wand) is wrapped in a sterile condom-like cover and inserted into the vagina. <p dir=ltr>The practitioner will then move the wand within the vaginal cavity to scan your uterus. You’ll feel pressure, but it should be painless.<p dir=ltr>The transducer emits soundwaves, which bounce off your baby to produce an image you can see on a computer or video screen. <h3 dir=ltr>Transabdominal ultrasound</h3><p dir=ltr>If your first ultrasound is after week 6 or 7, you'll likely get a transabdominal ultrasound. Gel is rubbed onto your belly to help the soundwaves move more easily. Then the wand is rubbed over your stomach to produce images of your baby.<p dir=ltr><span id=docs-internal-guid-c589bbd8-7fff-17ac-6181-b0657c0f872a>This exam shouldn’t hurt, although it can be somewhat uncomfortable (especially with a full bladder) if the sonographer needs to press hard on your abdomen to see a particular part of your baby more clearly.</span><h2 id=sonogram>What's the difference between a sonogram and an ultrasound?</h2><p dir=ltr>Though the words sonogram and ultrasound are often used interchangeably, there is a distinction:<ul><li dir=ltr><strong>Ultrasound</strong> is the term for an imaging test that uses sound to produce pictures.<li dir=ltr><strong>Sonogram</strong> is the picture produced by ultrasound technology.</ul><h2 id=risks>Do ultrasounds during pregnancy have any risks?</h2><p dir=ltr>Ultrasounds are noninvasive and very low-risk when performed by your health care practitioner. There is no set rule for how many ultrasounds are safe during pregnancy, but ACOG recommends sticking to just one to two ultrasounds in total (outside of other circumstances where more are medically necessary).<p dir=ltr>That said, some research has found that the average number of ultrasounds women are having is much higher than recommended — more than five over the course of pregnancy. <p dir=ltr>Both ACOG recommends that pregnant women avoid keepsake 3D and 4D sonograms marketed by private companies, along with <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/ask-heidi/fetal-heart-monitors.aspx>at-home fetal monitors</a>. While there's a lack of evidence of any harm due to ultrasound imaging and heartbeat monitors, there isn’t enough research to rule out any long-term effects.<p dir=ltr>What's more, although ultrasounds are usually relatively accurate at estimating a baby's size, they can also underestimate or overestimate weight, which may occasionally result in unnecessary C-sections or premature deliveries. <p dir=ltr>So if your doctor recommends more than two ultrasounds when you're expecting, don’t hesitate to ask questions to ensure that the extra ultrasounds are medically required.</p><br></div><div class="medical-authority py-4"><p>From the What to Expect editorial team and <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/about-heidi-murkoff/">Heidi Murkoff,</a> author of <em>What to Expect When You're Expecting</em>. class=new-jump-links__c__list__item__link__text><svg class=icon-location><use xlink:href=#location /></svg> How do you cope with separation anxiety in pregnancy?</div></a></ul></div></div></div></div><div class=article-body><p dir=ltr><strong>Pregnancy separation anxiety, which might feel like intense fear or distress when apart from a partner or support person, can be common when you're expecting. Hormonal shifts, emotional upheaval, and the stress of impending parenthood can all contribute to symptoms. Gradual exposure to time apart, breathing exercises, and therapy may help manage symptoms before and after birth.</strong><p dir=ltr>My husband is a big nature-loving guy. He often wakes up before sunrise and heads to the forest for a casual 9-mile hike, no big deal. So when he brought up going on an overnight backpacking trip, I was thrilled for him. Cut to the day he left for his trip: I spiraled into a full-blown panic attack, complete with shortness of breath, a racing heart, trembling, and intense fear. It was so bad I called my mom in tears.<div id=WhatToExpect_Slideshow data-primis-ad style=margin-top:20px;margin-bottom:20px><script>(function(){function loadPrimis(){var s=document.createElement("script");s.type="text/javascript";s.src="https://live.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?s=121100&cbuster=1782858575686&playerApiId=WhatToExpect_Slideshow";document.getElementById("WhatToExpect_Slideshow").appendChild(s);}
if(window.WTEAdInfo){loadPrimis();}else{window.addEventListener("WTEAdInfoReady",loadPrimis,{once:true});}})();</script></div><p dir=ltr>While I'm no stranger to panic attacks, this was far from the first time my husband and I had spent time apart over the years, and it never triggered my <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/anxiety/">anxiety</a> before. But this time, things felt different, scarier, and there's one big reason — I'm pregnant with our first baby. Spending time apart from my husband for an extended period while pregnant made me feel vulnerable in a way I hadn't experienced before, which triggered fear and anxiety that lingered until he returned. <p dir=ltr>I later learned a <a href="https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10431694/" target=_blank rel="">study</a> found that nearly 46% of pregnant women experienced significant adult separation anxiety disorder symptoms, mostly in their third trimester.<span id=1-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#1 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#1>National Institutes of Health</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>The Association of Dysfunctional Attitudes and Adult Separation Anxiety in Pregnancy: A Cross-Sectional Study</span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=1-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[1]</a></sup><p dir=ltr>So if this is something you can relate to, know that you're not alone. Keep reading to learn what experts want you to know about pregnancy separation anxiety, plus tips for coping with it. <p dir=ltr><section class=keytakeaways-c><div class=keytakeaways-c__header><div class=keytakeaways-c__header__summary-icon><img src=https://images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/redesign/key_takeaways.svg alt="summary icon" width=24 height=24></div><div class=keytakeaways-c__header__title>Key Takeaways</div></div><div class=keytakeaways-c__body><ul><li><strong>Separation anxiety during pregnancy</strong> <strong>is common. </strong>Research found that nearly half of pregnant women may experience symptoms, particularly in the third trimester.<li><strong>Moms-to-be with separation anxiety</strong> might have headaches, disrupted sleep, panic attacks, and heart palpitations.<li><strong>Coping strategies for separation anxiety in pregnancy</strong> include gradual exposure to time apart, deep breathing techniques, and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) if symptoms persist.</ul></div></section><h2 id=what>What is separation anxiety in pregnancy?</h2><p dir=ltr>Pregnancy separation anxiety is a type of adult separation anxiety (ASA), explains <a href="https://ladypartsdoctor.com/" target=_blank rel="">Stephanie Hack, M.D.</a>, MPH, a board-certified OB/GYN. It occurs when an adult experiences intense anxiety when separated from a loved one or close attachment figure, most often a partner. <p dir=ltr>Physical symptoms of pregnancy separation anxiety can include <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/symptoms-and-solutions/headaches-during-pregnancy.aspx>headaches</a>, stomachaches, <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/symptoms-and-solutions/insomnia.aspx>disrupted sleep</a>, and nightmares, Dr. Hack says.<p dir=ltr>These signs can overlap with other common <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/pregnancy-symptoms/" rel="">pregnancy symptoms</a>, but you might also feel uncontrollable worry or angst and have thoughts like "I can't live without my partner" or "I can't do things on my own," adds <a href="https://www.choosingtherapy.com/emily-guarnotta/" target=_blank rel="">Emily Guarnotta, Psy.D</a>., a licensed clinical psychologist.<p dir=ltr>"Since becoming pregnant, I’ve gotten separation anxiety from my partner," says <a href="https://community.whattoexpect.com/forums/" rel="">What to Expect Community</a> mom 19Tyler97. "Every time he leaves, I get emotional and cry."<p dir=ltr>Like with my case, separation anxiety can also trigger panic attacks — acute episodes of severe anxiety with physical symptoms such as sweating, difficulty breathing, and heart palpitations. All of these symptoms of pregnancy separation anxiety, Guarnotta says, can lead women to avoid leaving their partner's side. <h2 id=why>Why is separation anxiety so common during pregnancy?</h2><p dir=ltr>Transition periods can exacerbate separation anxiety, and pregnancy is without a doubt a life-changing transition.<p dir=ltr>"Being pregnant also sets us up for higher levels of baseline anxiety, and being separated from a support can push one over the edge," says <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/reviewers/sipra-laddha-44>Sipra Laddha, M.D.</a>, a reproductive psychiatrist and member of the <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/medical-review/">What to Expect Medical Review Board</a>. <p dir=ltr>The physical, emotional, and hormonal changes women experience during pregnancy can be disorienting. That coupled with the stress of preparing for parenthood can make expectant moms more vulnerable to experiencing mood or anxiety disorders. <p dir=ltr>Women who experience anxiety during pregnancy are also more likely to experience <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/postpartum-health-and-care/postpartum-anxiety/">anxiety postpartum</a> as well."These hormonal changes combined with sleep deprivation and the demands of caring for a newborn can contribute to developing postpartum separation anxiety," Guarnotta says. <h2 id=how>How can you cope with separation anxiety in pregnancy?</h2><h3 dir=ltr>Gradually ease into time apart</h3><p dir=ltr>Expose yourself to what makes you anxious, such as spending time away from your support person, suggests Dr. Hack. The key is to do it gradually, starting with short periods and increasing the length of time as you feel more comfortable.<p dir=ltr>Most importantly, do not avoid what makes you anxious, as it only reinforces anxiety. Though it may give you some temporary relief to avoid a trigger, avoidance typically worsens overall anxiety levels in the long run, Dr. Laddha says.<h3 dir=ltr>Learn and practice deep breathing skills</h3><p dir=ltr>Breathing deeply can help ease your symptoms when anxiety arises. "Deep breathing can get more oxygen into your body and activates the parasympathetic nervous system, which helps you recover from the fight-or-flight response," Guarnotta says. "To do this, take a four-second long inhale through your nose, hold, and then release the air through your mouth for six seconds."<h3 dir=ltr>Get help if symptoms persist </h3><p dir=ltr>Lastly, seek support from a therapist if needed. Therapy can get to the root of the separation anxiety, Guarnotta says. Specifically, she recommends <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/postpartum-health-and-care/types-of-therapy-postpartum-depression>cognitive behavioral therapy</a> (CBT), which can modify unhealthy beliefs contributing to separation anxiety. Getting support during pregnancy means you'll learn how to cope with separation anxiety if it occurs after birth as well. <p dir=ltr>If you're experiencing pregnancy separation anxiety, remember that you're not alone in your experience. Don't hesitate to reach out for support from loved ones or professionals when needed. <p dir=ltr>As for me, talking to my therapist and doubling down on self-care to soothe my nervous system has been a big help. I'm happy to report I entered my <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/third-trimester-of-pregnancy.aspx rel="">third trimester</a> feeling much more empowered and at ease. </p><br></div><div class="medical-authority py-4"><p>From the What to Expect editorial team and <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/about-heidi-murkoff/">Heidi Murkoff,</a> author of <em>What to Expect When You're Expecting</em>. Wearing light, loose clothing and keeping cool with air conditioning, cool or tepid baths, and cool, wet washcloths can soothe the itch of this annoying skin condition.</strong><p>Learn more about why heat rash happens during pregnancy and what you can do about it.<div id=WhatToExpect_Slideshow data-primis-ad style=margin-top:20px;margin-bottom:20px><script>(function(){function loadPrimis(){var s=document.createElement("script");s.type="text/javascript";s.src="https://live.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?s=121100&cbuster=1782858578234&playerApiId=WhatToExpect_Slideshow";document.getElementById("WhatToExpect_Slideshow").appendChild(s);}

Calamine lotion and talc-free powders may also provide relief.<li><strong>Most heat rashes are harmless, but persistent or severe symptoms should be checked by a doctor.</strong> See your doctor if the rash lasts more than a few days, becomes painful, shows signs of infection, or is accompanied by other concerning symptoms.</ul></div></section><h2 id=symptoms>What are the symptoms of heat rash during pregnancy?</h2><div class=media-c><img data-src='//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/heat-rash-skin-condition-2021-722x406.jpg?width=596' alt='heat rash' width=596 height=335 class='__lazy-load hero-img embed-image'><div class=caption-credit-c><div class=photo-credit>Science Source; iStock</div></div></div><p>Heat rash appears as pink or red, bug-bite-like bumps that can itch or feel prickly or sensitive. It can sometimes look like pimples and may even develop whiteheads.<span id=1-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#1 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#1>Mayo Clinic</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>Heat Rash</span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=1-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[1]</a></sup><p>You're most likely to see it in areas where <a href=../../../pregnancy/sweating>sweat</a> becomes trapped between the folds of your skin, such as:<ul><li>In the creases between and beneath the breasts<li>Where the bulge of the lower abdomen rubs against the top of the pubic area<li>On your back<li>On the inner thighs<li>On the armpits<li>In the creases of your elbows</ul><p>"I get heat rashes a LOT when pregnant!" says <a href="https://community.whattoexpect.com/forums/" target=_blank>What to Expect Community</a> member eclaire24. "Often on my thighs or under my boobs."<p>It can easily be confused with with other <a href=../../../pregnancy/symptoms-and-solutions/skin-changes.aspx>pregnancy-related skin conditions</a>, such as:<ul><li><strong>Hives,</strong> or itchy, raised welt-like bumps that can appear suddenly on the body, usually as an allergic reaction. Hives tend to last anywhere from a few days to a few weeks.<li><strong>Prurigo</strong>, which often appears as itchy, crusty bumps on your arms or legs, and can happen at any point in pregnancy.<li><strong>Pruritic folliculitis</strong>, which causes acne-like, pus-filled bumps that may appear on your torso and spread to your arms, chest, and back. It typically develops during the <a href=../../../second-trimester-of-pregnancy.aspx>second trimester</a> or <a href=../../../third-trimester-of-pregnancy.aspx>third trimester</a>.<li><strong>Pemphigoid gestationis</strong>, which is a rare autoimmune skin disorder that can suddenly pop up in the second or third trimester and cause a hive-like rash on your midsection that can turn into blisters.<li><strong>Cholestasis of pregnancy</strong>, which is an intense itch all over your body, particularly on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. It typically shows up in the third trimester and may be accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and jaundice (the whites of the eyes and skin may be yellow-colored). <a href=../../../pregnancy/your-health/cholestasis>Cholestasis</a> is not actually a rash — it's a sign of liver disease triggered by your hormones and should be evaluated by a doctor.<li><strong>Pustular psoriasis of pregnancy</strong>, which is a severe form of pustular psoriasis that appears as red, inflamed, crusty lesions — commonly on the thighs and groin — during the second half of pregnancy.<li><strong>Pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy (PUPPP)</strong>, which appears as itchy, red, raised skin patches on the stomach, often near <a href=../../../pregnancy/symptoms-and-solutions/stretch-marks.aspx>stretch marks</a>, and can spread to your limbs. <a href=../../../pregnancy/whose-body/skin-rashy.aspx>PUPPP</a> typically only develops in your first pregnancy, during the third trimester.</ul><h2 id=causes>What causes heat rash during pregnancy?</h2><p>Also known as prickly heat, heat rash happens when the sweat ducts in your pores become clogged, trapping perspiration beneath the skin. It tends to crop up during the hot, humid months.<div class=ad-container><span id=gptAd5track></span><div id=gptAd5 class="fast-ads content-ad" data-inview=true data-disabled=False data-adhesive=False></div></div><div><a class=app-to-web-promo href=https://wte.onelink.me/85iI/z7fc5p33 target=_blank rel=noopener> <img src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/my-journal-sep-2024.png data-src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/my-journal-sep-2024.png alt="" class=app-to-web-promo__image><div class=app-to-web-promo__title>Track your symptoms in the What to Expect app — and see what your body is telling you.</div><div class=app-to-web-promo__cheveron><img src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/redesign/chevron-right.svg data-src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/redesign/chevron-right.svg alt=""></div></a></div><p>Heat rash can be triggered by a combination of pregnancy-related changes: <a href="../../../news/pregnancy/pregnancy-safety-heat-wave/">increased body heat</a>, excessive perspiration, and friction from skin rubbing against itself or clothing. While it's not pretty, fortunately prickly heat is usually only slightly irritating.<p>"I am very prone to heat rash normally, so I expected it in pregnancy," says Community mom BoyMomEst2023. "But it came on so much faster than usual!"<p>Track your symptoms with the MyJournal tool in our free <a href=https://wte.onelink.me/85iI/7s0l3a5z target=_blank>What to Expect app</a>.<h2 id=treatment>How do I treat heat rash during pregnancy?</h2><p>Wondering how to beat the heat? There are plenty of pregnancy-safe ways to <a href="../../../baby-products/pregnancy/best-remedies-treating-itchy-skin-during-pregnancy/">soothe itchy skin</a> and help heal your heat rash.<ul><li><strong>Wear light, loose-fitting cotton clothes.</strong> To help minimize sweating and friction, avoid tight-fitting clothing and leggings. And choose your fabrics wisely — synthetic material can worsen sweating, and scratchy ones like wool can cause itching.<li><strong>Apply a cool, damp compress to your skin. </strong>To cool the rash, try soaking a washcloth in cold water or chilled green tea and applying it to the affected area for five minutes, three times a day.<li><strong>Rinse off. </strong>Take warm or tepid (not hot) baths and showers — and don't linger for too long, use harsh soaps, or make the water too hot. A tepid oatmeal bath can also be very soothing, as oatmeal contains compounds that relieve inflammation.<li><strong>Pat on powder.</strong> Sprinkle a bit of cornstarch or talc-free powder to absorb sweat during the day.<li><strong>Apply calamine lotion.</strong> It contains zinc oxide, which has soothing properties and can temporarily relieve itching as it dries.<li><strong>Turn on the air conditioning or a fan.</strong> This can help you avoid overheating, stay cool, and keep sweat at bay.<li><strong>Get naked.</strong> And stay that way whenever you can. Fresh air is the best antidote to heat rash.<li><strong>Ask your doctor about hydrocortisone cream.</strong> Many over-the-counter heat rash remedies contain hydrocortisone, a common anti-itch ingredient. But before you apply the medication, check with your dermatologist or pharmacist to make sure the ingredients are safe to use during pregnancy.</ul><p>"It was behind my knees and in my elbow crease," says Community mom OnlyaGeniousCouldLoveMe. "I used hydrocortisone cream. Went away in about a week and a half. No issues ever since!"<h2 id=no>What remedies don't work for pregnancy heat rash?</h2><p>You should steer clear of some treatments and products when you have heat rash during pregnancy, including:<ul><li><strong>Skin irritants. </strong>Stay away from perfumes, fragranced lotions, and harsh soaps.<li><strong>Petroleum-based ointments or mineral oil creams.</strong> Heavy creams or oils can worsen heat rash because they may further block sweat ducts.</ul><h2 id=doctor>When should I see a doctor about heat rash during pregnancy?</h2><p>Usually, heat rashes are harmless. But there are certain symptoms that may warrant a call to your doctor, including:<ul><li>If the rash or irritation lasts longer than a couple of days.<li>If you're experiencing pain or intense itching.<li>If the rash becomes infected — for example, it leaks pus or fluid, or is accompanied by symptoms like swelling, fever, and nausea.</ul><p>While it may not be pretty or comfortable, in all likelihood, your heat rash will fade within a few days — and be nothing more than a mild inconvenience.</p><br><div class=faq-container><div class=faq__header><div class=faq__header__title><h2>Heat Rash During Pregnancy FAQs</h2></div><div class=faq__header__line></div></div><div class="accordion faq-info-accordion" id=faqInfo><div class=card><div class=card-header><h4 data-toggle=collapse data-target=#question-5555-0 aria-expanded=false>How do you treat heat rash during pregnancy?
